\chapter*{Abstract}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Abstract}
\noindent
Air pollution in Indian cities regularly reaches hazardous concentrations,
and a forecast is useful only if it arrives before the hazardous day does.
This project forecasts daily PM2.5 one to three days ahead at a Delhi monitor
and evaluates the forecasts as a warning system rather than by average error
alone. The central finding is that the alarm budget a decision maker accepts
dominates the choice of model. Across ten specifications, from simple
benchmarks and a classical ARIMA model with annual Fourier terms to four
machine learning regressors and a recurrent network, the spread in hit rate
at a fixed alarm budget is about five percentage points, while moving the
budget from forty to one hundred alarms a year moves the hit rate by fifty.
Machine learning earns its place only partially. The classical model beats
every machine learning regressor at every horizon, a result strengthened
rather than weakened by a sensitivity analysis on the cleaning threshold, and
the one model that does win, a recurrent network, wins only at one day ahead,
reported as a range across ten seeds rather than a single favourable one.
Adding observed wind speed and temperature narrows the one-day gap further
but leaves two and three days a statistical tie, and the extra accuracy
moves the achievable hit rate at a fixed alarm budget by at most a point,
reinforcing rather than overturning the central finding above. Two
real defects in the source monitor, a clipped instrument ceiling and a
miscalculated coverage statistic, were diagnosed and corrected before
modelling began. The recommendation is to design a warning system around its
alarm budget, treating the forecasting model as a secondary refinement.

\chapter{Introduction}
\label{chap:intro}

\section{Research Background}

Air pollution in Indian cities regularly reaches concentrations classified as
hazardous to human health. Fine particulate matter small enough to be
classified as PM2.5 penetrates deep into the respiratory system, and
sustained epidemiological evidence links exposure to it with increased
cardiopulmonary and all-cause mortality \citep{pope2006health,chen2020mortality},
which is the reason a health threshold rather than an arbitrary concentration
is the event this project forecasts. The public response to such episodes depends on
knowing that a severe day is coming before it arrives: a forecast issued on
the morning of a hazardous day is of limited value, while one issued a day or
more ahead can change behaviour, whether through health advisories,
restrictions on outdoor activity, or school closures. Daily pollution series
carry structure that makes such forecasting feasible in principle: persistence
from one day to the next, a strong annual cycle driven by meteorology and
seasonal agricultural burning, and dependence on recent local conditions.

My interest in this question is also personal. Having grown up in India, air
pollution was not an abstract statistic but part of ordinary life: seasonal
smog that turned daylight hazy, and days when going outside meant a sore
throat. Whether those days can be predicted reliably enough to be worth
warning people about is a question I have a genuine stake in.

\section{Research Problem}

Existing machine learning studies of Indian air quality (reviewed in
Chapter~\ref{chap:lit}) report forecast accuracy by average error, and do not
decompose that accuracy by the operating point at which a warning would
actually be raised. A model with respectable average error can still be a
poor warning system if it systematically misses the extreme days that are the
only ones anyone cares about, and the reverse also holds: two models with
very different average error can produce nearly identical warning
performance once a decision threshold is applied. Separately, the project
this report was proposed under assumed that daily pollution series carry a
weekly cycle alongside the annual one, driven by traffic and industrial
activity, and treated reconciling two seasonal periods as a central modelling
difficulty. Neither assumption is safe to carry into the modelling without
testing it directly, and both are tested in this report.

\section{Research Objectives}

\begin{enumerate}
\item To develop and evaluate a suite of classical, machine learning, and
deep learning models for forecasting daily PM2.5 concentrations one to three
days ahead at a single, well-characterised Indian monitoring station, under
an evaluation protocol that cannot leak future information into past
forecasts.
\item To compare two formulations of the hazardous-day warning problem:
forecasting the concentration and applying a health threshold to it, against
classifying the exceedance event directly.
\item To quantify forecast skill as a warning system, using hit rate and
false alarm rate under a varying decision threshold, rather than relying on
average error alone, and to establish how much of that skill is attributable
to the choice of model versus the choice of decision threshold.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Research Questions}

\begin{enumerate}
\item How accurately can daily concentrations be forecast one to three days
ahead by machine learning, relative to classical and naive benchmarks?
\item Is it better to forecast the concentration and then apply a threshold, or
to classify the exceedance event directly?
\item Considered as a warning system, what hit rate and false alarm rate does
each approach achieve, and how does the decision threshold trade them off?
\end{enumerate}

The answer to the third question turns out to dominate the other two, and the
report is organised accordingly.

\section{Research Significance}

The practical significance of this work is in the design of hazardous air
quality warning systems: the finding that the decision threshold dominates
the choice of model, developed in Chapter~\ref{chap:results} and
Chapter~\ref{chap:discussion}, implies that the alarm budget a health
authority is willing to raise is a more consequential design decision than
the forecasting model behind it. The methodological significance lies in
applying a leakage-tested rolling-origin evaluation, rather than a single
train-test split, to a model suite spanning classical statistics, machine
learning, and a deep recurrent architecture, on a dataset small enough that
the comparison between method families is itself informative about where
each is reliable.

\section{Structure of the Report}

Chapter~\ref{chap:lit} reviews the literature on air quality forecasting,
classical and machine learning methods for time series, deep learning methods
for time series, and forecast verification as a warning system.
Chapter~\ref{chap:method} describes the data, the two defects found in it,
and the full mathematical specification of every model fitted, organised
into machine learning methods and deep learning methods as the chapter's two
central sections, followed by the rolling-origin evaluation protocol.
Chapter~\ref{chap:results} presents the results against the three research
questions. Chapter~\ref{chap:discussion} interprets those results and states
the project's limitations. Chapter~\ref{chap:conclusion} concludes and
proposes future work.

\chapter{Literature Review}
\label{chap:lit}

\section{Air Quality Forecasting: Challenges and Characteristics}

Daily particulate matter series present a specific set of statistical
challenges that distinguish them from the time series most forecasting
methods were developed against. The distribution of PM2.5 concentrations is
strongly right skewed, with a small number of extreme episodes, rather than
normally distributed around a stable mean; the series is strongly seasonal
at the annual scale; and the quantity of practical interest, whether a day
exceeds a health threshold, is a minority class, typically under a third of
days even at a severe site. These three properties motivate working in
logarithms rather than on the raw concentration scale (Section~\ref{sec:arima}),
motivate testing rather than assuming the seasonal structure present in the
series (Section~\ref{sec:weekly}), and motivate evaluating forecasts as a
warning system rather than by a single average-error statistic
(Section~\ref{sec:verification}).

\section{Classical and Machine Learning Methods for Time Series Forecasting}
\label{sec:lit-ml}

The classical approach to a series with this structure is an autoregressive
integrated moving average (ARIMA) model, in which a series is differenced to
stationarity and then modelled as a linear combination of its own past values
and past forecast errors, following the identification and estimation
methodology set out by \citet{box2008time}. Seasonal variants extend this by
one additional seasonal period, but a series with two seasonal periods, for
instance a weekly cycle and an annual one, cannot be accommodated by a single
seasonal ARIMA order, which is one of the two assumptions this project tests
directly rather than carrying over unexamined. The order itself is
conventionally chosen by an information-criterion search over a bounded grid
rather than fixed in advance, an approach formalised for routine use by
\citet{hyndman2008autoarima}; this project follows the same principle, an
explicit grid scored by the Akaike information criterion rather than a single
order asserted without justification (Section~\ref{sec:arima}). Where the
seasonal pattern itself is complex, for instance more than one period or a
period that does not divide the sampling interval evenly, Fourier terms
offer a compact way to carry it as a small number of exogenous regressors
rather than as a large seasonal order; \citet{delivera2011fourier} develop
this idea within an exponential smoothing framework for series with multiple
seasonal periods, and the same device, harmonic regressors at a fixed set of
frequencies, is the one this project uses to carry the annual cycle in an
ARIMA model's exogenous term (Section~\ref{sec:arima}).

Machine learning offers an alternative that does not assume a linear
relationship between a forecast and its predictors. Penalised linear
regression controls the variance of an ordinary least squares fit by
shrinking its coefficients, which matters when predictors are highly
correlated, as lagged and rolling-window features of the same series
necessarily are \citep{hoerl1970ridge}. Random forests and gradient boosting
both build on classification and regression trees \citep{breiman1984cart},
which recursively partition the feature space to minimise within-region
error, but combine many trees by two different mechanisms. A random forest
averages trees fitted independently to bootstrap-resampled data, a technique
named bootstrap aggregating, or bagging, and shown to reduce the variance of
an unstable predictor such as a tree without changing its bias
\citep{breiman1996bagging,breiman2001random}. Gradient boosting instead
fits an ensemble additively, each new tree correcting the residual error of
the ensemble so far; this traces to boosting algorithms that combine many
weak learners into a strong one by reweighting misclassified examples
\citep{freund1997adaboost}, which \citet{friedman2001gradient} reformulated
as stagewise functional gradient descent, the form implemented by the
histogram-based estimator used in this project (Section~\ref{sec:ml-methods})
and, in a widely used alternative implementation not used here, by
\textsc{XGBoost} \citep{chen2016xgboost}. None of these three machine
learning methods assumes stationarity, a seasonal order, or a linear
functional form, which is their appeal relative to ARIMA; their cost is that
they fit the function empirically from a necessarily finite sample, and
\citet{makridakis2020m4} report, across 100{,}000 series in the M4
forecasting competition, that this flexibility does not reliably translate
into an advantage over classical benchmarks on series of a few thousand
observations, which is the order of magnitude available in this project.
This was not a new finding when M4 confirmed it at scale:
\citet{makridakis2018statistical} had already reported the same pattern on
the smaller M3 dataset and argued that the forecasting community had adopted
machine learning methods faster than the evidence for their superiority had
accumulated, and \citet{siaminamini2018comparison} report a direct head-to-head
instance of it, an LSTM failing to beat ARIMA on a set of financial and
economic series very different in domain from this project's but identical
in being short relative to a deep network's capacity. The picture is not
uniformly negative for machine learning, however: in the M5 competition,
run on retail demand series with genuine exogenous and hierarchical
structure to exploit, gradient boosting methods won decisively
\citep{makridakis2022m5}. Read together, M4 and M5 suggest the deciding
factor is not machine learning versus classical methods in the abstract but
whether the series on offer gives a flexible method something structural to
exploit beyond what a classical model already captures; Chapter~\ref{chap:results}
revisits this reading directly; a single daily PM2.5 series with no
exogenous predictors is closer to the M4 setting than the M5 one, which is
the comparison this project's own result in Chapter~\ref{chap:results}
confirms rather than contradicts. A different strand of this literature
asks not which family wins outright but whether they can be combined:
\citet{zhang2003hybrid} fit a neural network to an ARIMA model's residuals
and report a gain over either model alone. This project does not pursue a
hybrid, evaluating the two families side by side instead, precisely so that
the comparison in Chapter~\ref{chap:results} is informative about which
family suits this series rather than obscured by a blend of both.

Whichever family is used, the comparison is only as trustworthy as the
procedure used to test it, a methodological point this project treats as
seriously as the choice of model. \citet{tashman2000outofsample} reviews decades of
out-of-sample forecasting evaluations and argues that a single train-test
split, still common practice at the time, understates how much accuracy
varies across time periods; \citet{hewamalage2023evaluation} revisit the
same concern two decades later and document the same pitfalls still
occurring routinely in applied forecasting work, including exactly the
single-split optimism this project found and corrected in
Section~\ref{sec:rolling}. The rolling-origin design adopted here
(Section~\ref{sec:rolling}) is this project's answer to both papers' shared
complaint. The accuracy measure itself is a related choice:
\citet{hyndman2006mase} propose the mean absolute scaled error specifically
because percentage errors are undefined when a series can be zero and
unstable when it is close to zero, and this project reports it alongside
the relative mean absolute error introduced in Section~\ref{sec:evalmeasures}
for exactly the reason their paper gives, that a scaled error's apparent
improvement can reflect a change in the series' own volatility rather than
a change in forecast skill, which is precisely what was found when the
single split was replaced by the rolling-origin harness.

\section{Deep Learning Methods for Time Series Forecasting}
\label{sec:lit-dl}

\subsection{The Deep Learning Landscape for Time Series}
\label{sec:lit-dl-landscape}

Before narrowing to the single architecture this project fits, it is worth
stating why the others on offer were not chosen, since "we used a recurrent
network" is a much weaker claim without the alternatives it was weighed
against. The simplest deep architecture is the multilayer perceptron (MLP),
a feedforward network shown to approximate any continuous function given
enough hidden units \citep{hornik1989universal}, applied to forecasting
since at least the 1990s \citep{zhang1998ann}. An MLP has no sense of
sequence order built in: it treats its input as an unordered feature vector,
so applying one to a time series means first constructing lagged and
rolling-window features exactly as Section~\ref{sec:features} already does
for the penalised regression and tree models. An MLP fed that table would
not be a meaningfully different model from those already in the suite; the
sequence-aware architectures below exist precisely to avoid depending on
which lags a human chose to hand-engineer.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) take the opposite approach, sliding a
learned kernel along the time axis to detect local patterns directly from
the raw sequence, originally developed for images
\citep{lecun1998cnn} and adapted to seasonal time series with trends
directly comparable to this project's own series \citep{liu2020cnn}. A
convolution's receptive field is fixed by its kernel width and depth, so
capturing a cycle as long as a year needs either a very deep stack or a
very wide kernel; this project's own annual cycle is instead handed to
every model directly as a small number of Fourier terms
(Section~\ref{sec:features}), which removes much of the advantage a CNN's
automatic pattern detection would otherwise offer here.

Transformer architectures, outside the time series domain, replace
recurrence altogether with self-attention, letting every timestep attend
directly to every other one rather than propagating information step by
step. Adaptations for multi-horizon time series forecasting do not always
make that same substitution outright: the Temporal Fusion Transformer
\citep{lim2021tft}, for instance, keeps a recurrent layer for local,
short-range processing and adds self-attention on top of it specifically
for long-range dependence and interpretability, a hybrid rather than a
wholesale replacement of recurrence. Either form carries the same
practical cost relative to a small GRU: a substantially larger parameter
count, tuned and validated on datasets several orders of magnitude larger
than the roughly three thousand daily observations available here. The
same sample-size argument Section~\ref{sec:lit-ml} makes against flexible
machine learning methods on a series this size applies with more force to
an architecture built for sequences of many thousands of tokens.

Weighed against all three, a recurrent network is the architecture whose
assumptions best match this project's data: it reads the sequence directly,
unlike an MLP; it is not limited to a fixed receptive field, unlike a CNN,
though that limitation matters less here given the Fourier terms already
carry the annual cycle; and it has a parameter count suited to a few
thousand observations, unlike a Transformer. Within the recurrent family,
the remaining choice is between a plain recurrent network and a gated one,
which the next two subsections address.

\subsection{Recurrent Neural Networks and the Vanishing Gradient Problem}

A recurrent neural network processes a sequence by maintaining a hidden
state that is updated at every timestep as a function of the current input
and the previous hidden state, which in principle lets it represent
dependence on the arbitrarily distant past without the fixed lag structure a
regression feature table imposes, trained by backpropagation through time, a
direct extension of the backpropagation algorithm for feedforward networks
\citep{rumelhart1986backprop}. In practice, a plain recurrent network trained
this way suffers from vanishing or exploding gradients as the sequence
lengthens: \citet{bengio1994vanishing} show formally that the conditions
which let a recurrent network store information robustly over many
timesteps are, under gradient descent, precisely the conditions under which
the gradient of a distant error with respect to an early input either
vanishes or explodes, so that reliably learning long-range dependence and
reliably training by gradient descent are in tension with each other.
\citet{hochreiter1997lstm} address this with the long short-term memory
(LSTM) architecture, a memory cell and three multiplicative gates
controlling what is written to, read from, and forgotten by that cell, at
the cost of a comparatively large number of parameters for a short daily
series.

\subsection{The Gated Recurrent Unit}

The gated recurrent unit (GRU) simplifies the LSTM to two gates and no
separate memory cell, while retaining the property that gradients can flow
across many timesteps without vanishing \citep{cho2014gru}. Its full
specification, and the specific architecture used in this project, is given
in Section~\ref{sec:gru}. The GRU's appeal for a daily series with roughly
three thousand observations is precisely its smaller parameter count relative
to an LSTM, which matters more on a dataset this size than the slightly
larger representational capacity an LSTM's extra gate and cell state provide.
\citet{lim2021survey} survey the broader move of deep learning into time
series forecasting of which the recurrent, convolutional and attention-based
families in Section~\ref{sec:lit-dl-landscape} are all part, and note that
the gain such architectures offer over classical methods depends heavily on
how much data and exogenous structure a given forecasting problem provides,
the same conditioning factor Section~\ref{sec:lit-ml} identifies as deciding
whether machine learning or a classical benchmark wins on a series of a
given size; this survey, and the general account of deep learning's
strengths and limits given by \citet{lecun2015deep}, frame the GRU result
in Chapter~\ref{chap:results} as an instance of a known pattern rather than
an isolated one. A practical limitation specific to
recurrent architectures, and directly relevant to this project's own series,
is that they require a value at every timestep and cannot represent a
missing observation natively; \citet{che2018rnn} study exactly this problem
for multivariate clinical time series and adopt the same device used in
Section~\ref{sec:gru}, carrying the last observed value forward alongside an
explicit missingness indicator, as a principled rather than ad hoc way to
hand a recurrent network a gap in its input.

\section{Machine Learning Applications to Delhi and Indian Air Quality}

Delhi's air pollution problem is well characterised at the level of sources
and policy before any forecasting model is applied to it.
\citet{guttikunda2014nature} review the emission inventory across major
Indian cities and identify vehicular traffic, industry, and seasonal biomass
burning as the dominant contributors, the last of which is the specific
mechanism behind the stubble burning season discussed below. Satellite-based
studies independently quantify that mechanism's contribution to Delhi's
severe episodes: \citet{cusworth2018quantifying} attribute a substantial
share of Delhi's post-monsoon particulate spikes to agricultural fires
further north, and \citet{jethva2019connecting} connect the same fires to
reduced regional air quality using more than a decade of satellite fire
counts. None of these three studies forecasts the series; they establish the
physical mechanism that a purely statistical model, such as every model in
this project, can only infer indirectly from the series' own seasonal
structure, which is worth stating plainly as a limitation of the
approach taken here.

Machine learning applied specifically to Delhi PM2.5 is not a new proposal.
\citet{masood2020delhi} fit two models, a support vector machine and an
artificial neural network, to predict Delhi's PM2.5 concentrations from
meteorological and pollutant covariates and report that the neural network
is the more accurate of the two; their inputs are exogenous measurements at
the forecast target day itself rather than the series' own lagged history,
which is a different forecasting problem from the one addressed here, where
the only inputs available at origin are the series' own past.
\citet{singh2025stubble} narrow the problem to Delhi's autumn stubble
burning season, when biomass burning in neighbouring states drives the
city's most severe episodes and, by their own account, its air pollutant
levels peak in October and November specifically. Their paper combines two
analyses rather than one: a health-risk assessment of stubble-season
exposure using a dedicated health-risk model, and, separately, a comparison
of three machine learning models, an artificial neural network, a support
vector machine, and a random forest, for PM2.5 forecasting, with the random
forest the most consistent of the three. The health-risk analysis and the
forecasting comparison sit alongside each other rather than one inside the
other: the forecasting models are themselves still scored by the same
average-error measures, $R^2$, RMSE and MAE, that this project argues are
insufficient on their own, not by a health-weighted criterion. Neither paper
evaluates its forecasts as a warning system in the sense used here, with an
explicit alarm budget and a false alarm rate reported alongside the hit
rate; both report accuracy on held-out data without decomposing it by the
operating point at
which an alarm would actually be raised. That gap, between forecast accuracy
and warning system performance, is the space this project's third research
question occupies.

The finding that a classical benchmark beats every machine learning model in
this project's own results (Chapter~\ref{chap:results}) is not an anomaly
against the wider forecasting literature discussed in
Section~\ref{sec:lit-ml}. The mechanism \citet{makridakis2020m4} propose,
that a few thousand observations is a small sample for a flexible learner
relative to the number of parameters a modern architecture can fit, applies
directly to a project with roughly three thousand daily observations. The
negative result for machine learning at two and three days ahead in
Chapter~\ref{chap:results} is therefore the expected outcome under that
literature rather than a surprise specific to this dataset.

\section{Forecast Verification as a Warning System}
\label{sec:verification}

The distinction this project draws between forecast accuracy and warning
system performance, hit rate, false alarm rate, and the trade-off between
them as the decision threshold moves, follows the verification framework
standard in operational meteorology \citep{jolliffe2012forecast}. That
literature developed around exactly the situation faced here: a forecast of
a rare, high-impact event, where the average error of a model is a poor
guide to its value as a warning, and where a contingency table decomposed by
decision threshold is more informative than any single accuracy score. Its
central methodological point, that verification measures should be chosen to
match the decision a forecast supports rather than borrowed by default from
a different problem, motivated reporting hit rate and false alarm rate as a
pair in Section~\ref{sec:evalmeasures} rather than a single skill score. The
critical success index reported alongside them, the fraction of forecast or
observed events that were correctly forecast, with correct quiet days
excluded from both numerator and denominator, was introduced by
\citet{schaefer1990csi} specifically to avoid a statistic inflated by the
large number of quiet days that dominate a rare-event problem such as this
one, where fewer than a third of days exceed the health threshold.

That same imbalance, a minority of hazardous days against a majority of
quiet ones, is the reason this project never reports plain classification
accuracy as a warning-system measure. \citet{he2009imbalance} survey the
broader problem of learning from imbalanced data and document how a
classifier can score highly on overall accuracy by predicting the majority
class essentially always, a failure mode this project's own alarm-budget
framing (Section~\ref{sec:evalmeasures}) is designed to make visible rather
than hide, since an alarm budget of zero would trivially achieve a hit rate
of zero rather than a flattering accuracy figure. \citet{saito2015prplot}
make the related point that a receiver operating characteristic curve, a
common default for a binary classifier, can look similarly optimistic on
imbalanced data because it is insensitive to a large true-negative count
that costs nothing to accumulate; a precision-recall-style decomposition, of
which the hit rate and false alarm rate pair used throughout this report is
a close relative, is the more informative choice for exactly this kind of
problem.

\section{Data Quality in Reference Air Quality Monitors}

The data quality problems documented in Section~\ref{sec:defects} are not
unique to this station. \citet{jiang2023negative} address the companion
problem to the one found here: reference monitors occasionally report
physically impossible negative PM2.5 concentrations, arising from instrument
noise near zero rather than a true measurement, and propose a defensible
statistical threshold below which a reading should be treated as invalid
rather than retained or naively clipped to zero. Their approach and the one
used in Section~\ref{sec:defects} for the clipped ceiling at 1990 share a
method rather than a target: both treat an implausible value as a data
quality question to be settled by evidence, specifically its relationship to
the plausible range and its recurrence pattern, rather than by a rule of
thumb applied uniformly. Considered together, artefacts at both ends of the
distribution suggest that reference-grade air quality monitors carry
systematic measurement pathologies that a forecasting study must
characterise explicitly rather than assume away.

A third data quality question, separate from an implausible value being
present, is a plausible value being absent. \citet{little2019missing} set
out the standard framework for reasoning about why data are missing, missing
completely at random, missing at random given other observed information, or
missing in a way that depends on the unobserved value itself, and show that
the appropriate treatment differs sharply between the three. The coverage
rule adopted in Section~\ref{sec:defects}, excluding a day when too few
readings contributed to its mean, is a judgement that the gaps here are
closer to the first two categories than the third: nothing in the station's
own account of why a reading is missing suggests that a reading is more
likely to be dropped specifically when the true concentration is unusually
high or low, as opposed to for reasons such as instrument maintenance that
are unrelated to the pollution level itself. The remaining short gaps that
survive the coverage rule are carried forward rather than discarded, using
the same forward-fill-plus-indicator treatment discussed for the recurrent
network in Section~\ref{sec:gru}, which is defensible under the same
assumption.

\section{Research Gap and Chapter Summary}

This chapter has covered five bodies of literature: the statistical
characteristics of air quality series that motivate the methodological
choices in Chapter~\ref{chap:method}; classical and machine learning methods
for time series forecasting, their shared lineage through bagging, boosting
and regression trees, and why the forecasting-competition literature
predicts a flexible learner need not beat a classical benchmark on a small
sample, together with the methodology for testing that comparison honestly,
out-of-sample evaluation and scale-free accuracy measures, rather than
taking any single reported number at face value; deep learning methods for
sequences, the wider landscape of feedforward, convolutional and
attention-based architectures weighed against the recurrent family before
narrowing to it, the specific architectural reason a GRU rather than an
LSTM suits a dataset this size, and the structural limitation, an inability
to represent a missing input, that a recurrent architecture carries
regardless of which gated variant is chosen; the physical background and
Delhi-specific forecasting literature, emission sources, biomass burning,
and two prior machine learning studies on this same city's PM2.5, that
motivates treating this as a hazard-warning problem rather than a
curve-fitting exercise and locates the gap, warning-system evaluation
against an explicit alarm budget, that those studies leave open; and the
two literatures, forecast
verification and air quality monitor data quality, that this project's own
findings connect back to directly. Taken together, this literature places
the project's contribution precisely. Applying an established model suite to
Delhi's air quality problem is not new, and neither is the finding that
classical methods hold their ground against machine learning on a modest
sample. What the Delhi-specific studies above do not do is evaluate that
comparison as a warning system with an explicit, varying alarm budget, using
verification methodology from a literature that reaches air quality
forecasting only indirectly. Chapter~\ref{chap:results} shows why that
omission matters: the ranking of models looks different once accuracy is
separated from operational usefulness, a finding neither literature taken
alone would have anticipated.

\chapter{Methodology}
\label{chap:method}

\section{Research Design}

This chapter proceeds from data to model to evaluation. Section~\ref{sec:data}
describes the data source and the station-selection process.
Section~\ref{sec:preprocess} describes two defects found in the raw series,
the seasonality analysis that overturned an assumption in the approved
proposal, and the feature table built from the cleaned series.
Section~\ref{sec:ml-methods} and Section~\ref{sec:dl-methods} give the full
mathematical specification of the two families of model this project
compares, machine learning and deep learning, each covering the method's
general form before the specific configuration used here.
Section~\ref{sec:rolling} specifies the rolling-origin evaluation every model
is scored under, and Section~\ref{sec:evalmeasures} specifies the accuracy
and warning-system measures reported in Chapter~\ref{chap:results}.

\section{Data Collection and Station Selection}
\label{sec:data}

Daily mean PM$_{2.5}$ concentrations were obtained from OpenAQ. Five candidate
monitoring stations within 25\,km of central Delhi were compared on data
coverage rather than on nominal length of record.

The comparison produced an unexpected constraint. Every station operated by the
Central Pollution Control Board returns measurements only from 19 February 2025,
approximately eighteen months, although the OpenAQ location metadata advertises a
first observation in February 2016. Four independent stations sharing an
identical cutoff indicates a systematic limit on what the measurements endpoint
serves rather than a coincidence. Only location 8118 returns the full record and
it was therefore selected.

This carries a limitation that must be stated plainly. Location 8118 is supplied
through AirNow and is a United States diplomatic post monitor rather than part of
the Indian official network. The project therefore forecasts at a single
well-characterised reference site in Delhi, which is common in this literature,
and the results should not be read as representative of the city as a whole.

\section{Data Preprocessing}
\label{sec:preprocess}

\subsection{Data Cleaning: Two Defects in the Source Data}
\label{sec:defects}

Two problems were identified before any modelling, one of which was silently
corrupting the series.

\paragraph{Physically impossible values.} The raw series contained five negative
concentrations and a maximum of 1990\,\textmu g\,m$^{-3}$. The value 1990.0
appeared three times identically on unrelated dates, which is the signature of a
clipped instrument ceiling rather than a measurement. One occurrence fell on 2
September, during the monsoon, between neighbouring days of 42 and 178.

\paragraph{An incorrect coverage denominator.} OpenAQ reports the completeness of
each daily aggregate as the observation count divided by an expected count of 24,
assuming hourly reporting. The sensor at location 8118 reported half-hourly from
2016 to 2024 and hourly from 2025 onward. The visible symptom is a reported
completeness exceeding 100 per cent, which is impossible. The damaging symptom is
invisible: a day holding 24 of a genuine 48 readings is scored as fully complete,
so a mean computed from half a day of a polluted afternoon enters the series as
though it were a daily mean. Days at 50 to 75 per cent true coverage produced
implausible values approximately seven times as often as days above 90 per cent,
which identifies incomplete days as the mechanism rather than a coincidence.

The correction takes the reporting cadence from the data, using the ninetieth
percentile of observation counts within each year, which follows the 2025 change
in reporting interval automatically. Recomputed on that basis, 1{,}085 of the
3{,}467 raw calendar-linked days fall below 75 per cent true coverage, far more
than the 268 days that have no recorded value at all and would be the only ones
flagged by a check for whether a value exists rather than how reliably it was
measured.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Cleaning rules applied, and the basis for each.}
\label{tab:cleaning}
\input{tables/cleaning}
\end{table}

The coverage threshold is set at 50 per cent rather than a stricter value because
the longest gap is the binding constraint: at 60 per cent the worst gap rises to
69 days and at 90 per cent to 185 days, either of which would distort estimation
of the annual cycle. At 50 per cent the worst gap is 34 days. The exceedance rate
moves only from 30.0 to 27.0 per cent across every candidate threshold, which
confirms that the filter is not selectively removing the events of interest.

\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig2_coverage}
\caption{The coverage defect. Panel (a) shows the number of readings contributing
to each daily mean, with the cadence estimated from the data each year as the
solid line and the fixed denominator of 24 as the dashed line. Panel (b) shows
the rate of implausible values by true coverage.}
\label{fig:coverage}
\end{figure}

\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_series}
\caption{The cleaned daily series, with days exceeding the threshold shaded. The
episodic structure is the feature the project sets out to forecast: exceedances
arrive as multi-day winter episodes rather than as isolated days.}
