\subsection{Seasonality Analysis}
\label{sec:weekly}

The approved proposal states that daily pollution series carry a weekly cycle
driven by traffic and industrial activity, and treats the coexistence of a weekly
and an annual period as the central modelling difficulty, since a seasonal ARIMA
accommodates only one seasonal period.

Tested on the cleaned series, the weekly cycle is not present at this station.
Three independent tests agree, each asking a different kind of question of
the same series: whether its variance concentrates at a weekly frequency,
whether a lag-7 dependency survives beyond what the series' own short-range
decay would produce anyway, and whether the day of the week carries a mean
effect.

The periodogram estimates how a series' variance decomposes across
frequency, from the magnitude of its discrete Fourier transform at each
Fourier frequency $\omega_j = 2\pi j/n$,
\begin{equation}
I(\omega_j) \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\left[\Big(\sum_{t=1}^{n} y_t\cos(\omega_j t)\Big)^2
\;+\; \Big(\sum_{t=1}^{n} y_t\sin(\omega_j t)\Big)^2\right],
\label{eq:periodogram}
\end{equation}
read as a period of $n/j$ days rather than a frequency. It gives dominant
periods of 357.9, 178.9, 188.4, 397.7, 325.4 and 60.7 days, which is the
annual cycle and its harmonics, with nothing near seven.

On the deseasonalised logarithm of concentration, the sample autocorrelation
at lag $k$,
\begin{equation}
\hat\rho_k \;=\; \frac{\sum_{t=k+1}^{n}(y_t-\bar y)(y_{t-k}-\bar y)}
{\sum_{t=1}^{n}(y_t-\bar y)^2},
\label{eq:acf}
\end{equation}
is 0.173 at lag 7, while lag 6 is 0.179 and lag 8 is 0.153, so lag 7 lies on
the decay curve rather than above it; the same holds at lags 14 and 21. A
genuine weekly effect would show as a spike at lag 7 breaking that otherwise
smooth decay, not merely as some nonzero value, since every short lag is
autocorrelated regardless of any seasonal structure at all.

The day of week effect on the same residuals spans 6.5 per cent between the
highest and lowest day. A one-way analysis of variance tests whether the
seven day-of-week group means differ by more than the scatter within each
group predicts,
\begin{equation}
F \;=\; \frac{\sum_{g=1}^{7} n_g(\bar y_g - \bar y)^2 \,/\, (7-1)}
{\sum_{g=1}^{7}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}(y_{gi} - \bar y_g)^2 \,/\, (n-7)},
\label{eq:anova}
\end{equation}
giving $F = 1.13$, $p = 0.34$ against an $F_{6,\,n-7}$ reference
distribution, and a Kruskal-Wallis test,
\begin{equation}
H \;=\; \frac{12}{n(n+1)}\sum_{g=1}^{7}\frac{R_g^2}{n_g} \;-\; 3(n+1),
\label{eq:kruskalwallis}
\end{equation}
the same comparison on each observation's rank summed within group $g$,
$R_g$, rather than on the residual directly, asymptotically $\chi^2_6$ under
the null and free of the normal-residual assumption Equation~\ref{eq:anova}
makes, gives $p = 0.77$. Three tests built on different assumptions, a
spectral decomposition, a linear-model F-test, and a distribution-free
rank test, agreeing is what makes the absence convincing rather than an
artefact of one test's particular assumptions failing to hold here.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig3_weekly}
\caption{No weekly cycle. Lags 7, 14 and 21 are circled and lie on the decay
curve rather than above it. Every day of week interval contains zero.}
\label{fig:weekly}
\end{figure}

There is a physical reading rather than a null result. A weekly rhythm in urban
particulate concentration is a traffic signature, and location 8118 sits in the
diplomatic enclave rather than at a roadside site such as ITO or Anand Vihar. Its
absence at a site that is not traffic dominated is what one would expect.

The consequence for the specification is direct: the classical benchmark is ARIMA
with annual Fourier terms as exogenous regressors and no weekly seasonal order.
The specification is simpler, better identified, and empirically justified rather
than assumed.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.66\textwidth]{figures/fig4_annual}
\caption{The annual cycle, by contrast, is unmistakable: monthly median with the
interquartile range shaded. Its strength is what makes the absence in
Figure~\ref{fig:weekly} credible rather than an artefact of a weak test.}
\label{fig:annual}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Feature Construction}
\label{sec:features}

A supervised table was built with one row per forecast origin. A row indexed by
date $t$ carries only functions of observations up to and including day $t$, and
its targets are the concentrations on days $t+1$, $t+2$ and $t+3$. Features
comprise lags at 0, 1, 2, 3 and 7 days; first differences; rolling mean, standard
deviation and maximum over 3, 7, 14 and 30 days; an anomaly and standardised
anomaly against the 30 day norm; exceedance frequency over the last 7 and 30
days; days since the last exceedance; calendar terms; four pairs of annual
Fourier terms; and three missingness indicators.

Missing values are never imputed. Gradient boosting accepts them natively and the
state space models skip the measurement update at a gap, so the absence is
carried as information rather than replaced by a fabricated value. The single
exception is the recurrent network, discussed in Section~\ref{sec:gru}.

\subsection{Weather Covariates}
\label{sec:weather}

The feature table above is extended with daily surface weather for the same
station coordinates, fetched through the \texttt{meteostat} package, which
aggregates NOAA and GHCN-Daily records. Six variables are available at
reasonable completeness: mean, minimum and maximum temperature, wind speed,
mean sea level pressure, and precipitation. Each enters the table at its own
value, its value one day earlier, and its three day rolling mean, so that a
model can use both the current reading and its recent trend. Every weather
column obeys the same rule as every other feature in this table: only
observations up to and including day $t$ are used. A real early-warning
system would use a numerical weather \emph{forecast} for the days ahead
rather than the weather already observed, which would very likely help
further, but that is a materially stronger claim about what is knowable at
the forecast origin, and this project does not make it.

The weather record carries its own data quality defect, a third one for this
project, and it was diagnosed the same way as the two in
Section~\ref{sec:defects}: checked directly rather than assumed. Within the
window it covers, the record is close to complete, 99.9 per cent for
temperature and 99.6 per cent for wind speed. But that window ends 202 days
before the PM2.5 series does: the station's archive is current only to
reporting delays of several months, a different failure mode from the two
already documented, a hard cutoff rather than scattered gaps. Precipitation
is worse, with only 54 per cent coverage even before that cutoff, and is
excluded from the recurrent network's channels for this reason, retained only
for the tree models, which take a sparse column natively rather than needing
it imputed.

That cutoff means a meaningful share of the rolling-origin test period in
Section~\ref{sec:rolling} carries no weather observation at the forecast
origin. Rather than let that pass silently, the comparison in
Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1} is checked twice: once over every origin, where
the gap is handled exactly as every other missing value in this project is,
left as \texttt{NaN} for gradient boosting, imputed from the training window
for ridge and the random forest, and carried forward with a missingness flag
for the recurrent network, and once restricted to origins that fall entirely
inside the window where weather is genuinely observed. The two give the same
answer, which is what makes the first trustworthy.

\section{Classical and Machine Learning Methods}
\label{sec:ml-methods}

Six of the ten specifications fitted in this project belong to the machine
learning family in the broad sense used in Section~\ref{sec:lit-ml}: the
classical ARIMA benchmark, which is included here for comparison even though
it predates the term, and the three explicitly machine learning regressors,
each fitted to both the level of concentration and its change from the
forecast origin. Every model in this section is fitted to the logarithm of
concentration rather than the raw scale. Annual Fourier terms explain 69 per
cent of the variance of the logarithm against considerably less on the raw
scale, and fitting in logs prevents a model predicting a negative
concentration, which has no physical meaning.

\subsection{Classical Benchmark: ARIMA with Fourier Terms}
\label{sec:arima}

Let $y_t = \log(\text{PM2.5}_t)$ and let $B$ denote the backshift operator,
$B y_t = y_{t-1}$. Following the Box-Jenkins formulation \citep{box2008time},
an autoregressive integrated moving average model of order $(p,d,q)$ with
exogenous regressors $x_t$ is
\begin{equation}
\phi(B)\,(1-B)^d y_t \;=\; c \;+\; \theta(B)\,\varepsilon_t \;+\; \beta^\top x_t,
\label{eq:arima}
\end{equation}
where $\phi(B) = 1 - \phi_1 B - \cdots - \phi_p B^p$ is the autoregressive
polynomial, $\theta(B) = 1 + \theta_1 B + \cdots + \theta_q B^q$ is the moving
average polynomial, and $\varepsilon_t$ is white noise. The order is chosen
from an explicit grid of candidate $(p,d,q)$ triples by the Akaike
information criterion,
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{AIC} \;=\; -2\ln\hat L \;+\; 2k,
\label{eq:aic}
\end{equation}
where $\hat L$ is the model's maximised likelihood and $k$ its number of
free parameters, so the criterion rewards fit while charging a fixed penalty
for every additional parameter rather than letting the largest model in the
grid win by construction. The order scoring lowest on the training block is
$(p,d,q) = (1,1,1)$, AIC 1892.5, with the next best candidate in the grid,
$(1,1,2)$, at 1893.6: a gap of 1.1, too small to call $(1,1,1)$ decisively
better rather than a more parsimonious specification of roughly equal
support, which is the more defensible reading of why it was selected.
Equation~\ref{eq:arima} specialises to
\begin{equation}
(1 - \phi_1 B)(1-B)\,y_t \;=\; c \;+\; (1+\theta_1 B)\,\varepsilon_t \;+\;
\sum_{k=1}^{4}\Big[\alpha_k \sin\!\Big(\tfrac{2\pi k t}{365.25}\Big) +
\beta_k \cos\!\Big(\tfrac{2\pi k t}{365.25}\Big)\Big],
\label{eq:arima-fourier}
\end{equation}
with four pairs of annual Fourier terms ($K=4$) as the exogenous regressors
$x_t$, carrying the annual cycle established in Section~\ref{sec:weekly} and
deliberately carrying no weekly seasonal order. Fitted on the training
block, $\hat\phi_1 = 0.581$ and $\hat\theta_1 = -0.987$. Both must satisfy
$|\phi_1| < 1$ and $|\theta_1| < 1$ for the differenced series to be
stationary and the model invertible, the conditions under which an ARMA
process has the causal, one-sided representation Box-Jenkins estimation
assumes \citep{box2008time}; the fit satisfies both, although $\hat\theta_1$
sits only 0.013 inside its boundary, a near-cancellation between the
differencing and the moving average term that is a known signature of a
series close to overdifferenced rather than evidence the order search chose
badly, since $(1,1,1)$ still scored lowest of every order in the grid. The
implementation used here does not constrain the optimiser to this region,
\texttt{enforce\_stationarity=False} and \texttt{enforce\_invertibility=False}
in the SARIMAX call, so satisfying both conditions is a property of the
fitted optimum on this data rather than one guaranteed by construction.

That pair of values is a snapshot rather than a constant. The
rolling-origin evaluation behind every number in
Chapter~\ref{chap:results} re-estimates this same fixed order twenty-eight
times as the training window expands, every 90 days from 2019 to 2026,
and the coefficients move over that span rather than settling
immediately. $\hat\phi_1$ ranges from 0.520 at the first refit to 0.591
near the last, comfortably inside the stationarity boundary throughout.
$\hat\theta_1$ is less comfortable: from 2023 onward it stays within
0.012 to 0.014 of the invertibility boundary, matching the value reported
above, but at three of the twenty-eight refits, every one with fewer than
1{,}700 training days, the fitted value crosses the boundary outright,
$-1.006$, $-1.011$ and $-1.013$. The optimiser is not constrained to avoid
this, so a forecast is still produced and still scored at those refits
exactly as at any other; the single pair reported above describes the
model this evaluation settles into for most of its span, not a property
holding at every refit within it.

Using trigonometric
regressors at a fixed set of frequencies to carry a seasonal pattern inside
an otherwise standard model, rather than through a seasonal differencing
order, follows the same logic \citet{delivera2011fourier} apply to
exponential smoothing for series with seasonal patterns too complex for a
single seasonal order to represent; here the device is used to keep the
annual cycle outside the ARIMA order entirely, which is what makes carrying
no weekly term in parallel straightforward rather than a second seasonal
order fighting the first.

Back-transformation from the log scale is not innocent. If $\log y$ has
forecast mean $m$ and forecast variance $s^2$, then under the model's
Gaussian error assumption $y$ is lognormally distributed, and
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{median}(y) = \exp(m), \qquad \mathrm{mean}(y) = \exp\!\big(m + \tfrac{1}{2}s^2\big).
\label{eq:lognormal}
\end{equation}
Both quantities were produced as separately named models, since a report
that back-transforms without stating which one it reports has silently
changed what is being forecast. The gap between the two, and specifically
the tendency of the median variant to systematically under-forecast a
right-skewed quantity, is a known bias rather than a property special to
this project: \citet{miller1984bias} derive the same correction term,
$\exp(\tfrac{1}{2}s^2)$ in Equation~\ref{eq:lognormal}, for curve-fitting
contexts generally, as the adjustment needed to recover an unbiased mean
from a model fitted on the logarithm of a quantity.

\subsection{Penalised Linear Regression}

Given the feature matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ built in
Section~\ref{sec:features} and the target vector $y$, ordinary least squares
is unstable when predictors are highly correlated, as lagged and
rolling-window features of the same series necessarily are. Ridge regression
\citep{hoerl1970ridge} controls this by penalising the size of the
coefficient vector:
\begin{equation}
\hat\beta \;=\; \arg\min_{\beta} \; \|y - X\beta\|_2^2 \;+\; \lambda \|\beta\|_2^2,
\label{eq:ridge}
\end{equation}
Unlike every other regressor in this section, Equation~\ref{eq:ridge} has a
closed-form minimiser rather than one found by an iterative search. Writing
the objective as $J(\beta) = (y-X\beta)^\top(y-X\beta) + \lambda\beta^\top\beta$
and differentiating with respect to $\beta$,
\begin{equation}
\nabla_\beta J \;=\; -2X^\top(y-X\beta) \;+\; 2\lambda\beta,
\label{eq:ridge-grad}
\end{equation}
setting Equation~\ref{eq:ridge-grad} to zero gives the penalised normal
equations, $(X^\top X + \lambda I)\hat\beta = X^\top y$, so
\begin{equation}
\hat\beta \;=\; (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y.
\label{eq:ridge-solution}
\end{equation}
$X^\top X + \lambda I$ is positive definite for any $\lambda > 0$ even when
$X^\top X$ itself is singular or near singular, which is exactly the
collinear case the opening sentence of this subsection describes, so
Equation~\ref{eq:ridge-solution} exists and is unique where the ordinary
least squares solution, $\lambda = 0$, may not. The penalty $\lambda > 0$
shrinks the coefficients toward zero, trading a small increase in bias for
a reduction in variance; $\lambda$ is selected by cross-validation on the
training block at every refit.

\subsection{Random Forest}

A random forest \citep{breiman2001random} fits $B$ regression trees to
independent bootstrap resamples of the training data, each tree considering
only a random subset of features at every split, and averages their
predictions. Averaging over bootstrap resamples in this way is bootstrap
aggregating, or bagging \citep{breiman1996bagging}; a random forest adds the
random feature subset at each split on top of bagging specifically to
decorrelate the resulting trees further, since trees grown on overlapping
bootstrap samples of the same series would otherwise tend to split on the
same dominant lag features and average out less variance than independent
trees would:
\begin{equation}
\hat f(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B} T_b(x).
\label{eq:rf}
\end{equation}
Why decorrelation matters beyond bagging alone follows from the variance of
an average of $B$ identically distributed but not independent predictors,
each with variance $\sigma^2$ and pairwise correlation $\rho$,
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Var}\big(\hat f(x)\big) \;=\; \rho\sigma^2 \;+\; \frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2,
\label{eq:rf-variance}
\end{equation}
the bound \citet{breiman2001random} derives as the reason a random forest
can outperform plain bagging rather than merely matching it. The second
term in Equation~\ref{eq:rf-variance} vanishes as $B$ grows, but the first
does not, so $\rho\sigma^2$ is a floor that averaging alone, however many
trees, cannot fall below. Bagging without the random feature subset still
has every tree free to split on whichever lag dominates, which keeps $\rho$
high; restricting each split to a random subset of features is specifically
what lowers $\rho$, and with it the floor itself, a mechanism unrelated to
how many trees are averaged.

Each tree $T_b$ is grown by recursively partitioning the feature space: at a
node with data $\{(x_i,y_i)\}$, the split $(j,s)$ on feature $j$ at threshold
$s$ is chosen to minimise the total within-region sum of squared error,
\begin{equation}
\min_{j,s} \; \left[ \sum_{i\,:\,x_{ij} \le s} (y_i - \bar y_{R_1})^2 \;+\;
\sum_{i\,:\,x_{ij} > s} (y_i - \bar y_{R_2})^2 \right],
\label{eq:rf-split}
\end{equation}
where $R_1$ and $R_2$ are the two resulting regions and $\bar y_{R_1}$,
$\bar y_{R_2}$ their mean targets, the splitting rule set out for
classification and regression trees generally and collected in
\citet{breiman1984cart}.
Averaging over many such trees, each trained on a different resample and a
different random subset of features at each split, reduces the variance of a
single tree's prediction without imposing a linear functional form.

\subsection{Histogram Gradient Boosting}

Gradient boosting \citep{friedman2001gradient} fits an ensemble additively
rather than by averaging independent trees, generalising an older idea,
boosting, in which many weak learners are combined into one strong learner
by repeatedly reweighting the examples a classifier got wrong so that the
next learner in the sequence focuses on them \citep{freund1997adaboost}.
Friedman's reformulation recasts that reweighting as gradient descent in
function space rather than in the space of example weights, which is what
lets the same framework cover arbitrary differentiable loss functions rather
than only classification error. The justification is a first-order Taylor
expansion of the loss around the current ensemble $F_{m-1}$, treating the
update $h$ added at that point as the variable being optimised,
\begin{equation}
L\big(y_i, F_{m-1}(x_i) + h(x_i)\big) \;\approx\; L\big(y_i, F_{m-1}(x_i)\big)
\;+\; h(x_i)\left[\frac{\partial L(y_i,F(x_i))}{\partial F(x_i)}\right]_{F=F_{m-1}},
\label{eq:boost-taylor}
\end{equation}
which, to this linear order, is decreased fastest for a step of fixed size
by setting $h(x_i)$ in the direction opposite the bracketed gradient at
every training point: an infinite-dimensional analogue of ordinary gradient
descent, with one coordinate per training example rather than one per
model parameter, which is the sense in which this is descent in function
space rather than in the space of example weights. Fitting the gradient
exactly at every training point would reproduce the training data and
generalise nowhere, so the update is instead constrained to be a regression
tree, fitted not to the gradient itself but to its value at the training
points, the pseudo-residual
\begin{equation}
r_{im} \;=\; -\left[\frac{\partial L(y_i,F(x_i))}{\partial F(x_i)}\right]_{F=F_{m-1}},
\label{eq:grad-residual}
\end{equation}
The ensemble is initialised as a
constant, $F_0(x) = \arg\min_{\gamma} \sum_i L(y_i,\gamma)$, and for
$m = 1,\dots,M$ a regression tree $h_m$ is fitted to this target, which for
squared-error loss reduces to the ordinary residual
$r_{im} = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i)$, and the ensemble is updated by
\begin{equation}
F_m(x) \;=\; F_{m-1}(x) \;+\; \nu\, h_m(x),
\label{eq:boost-update}
\end{equation}
where $0 < \nu \le 1$ is a shrinkage (learning rate) parameter that controls
how much each new tree is allowed to correct the ensemble. The
histogram-based implementation used here bins continuous features before
searching for splits, which accepts missing values natively, consistent with
the decision in Section~\ref{sec:features} never to impute. This is the same
binning strategy that made gradient boosting practical on large tabular
datasets in implementations such as \textsc{XGBoost} \citep{chen2016xgboost};
scikit-learn's histogram-based estimator used here applies the same idea at
the scale this project needs, a few thousand rows rather than millions, so
the speed advantage that motivated the original design matters less here
than the fact that it accepts missing values without a separate imputation
step. Both the number
of boosting iterations $M$ and the per-tree leaf count were chosen at every
refit from a small explicit grid, since an uncontrolled $M$ overfits badly on
a series of this length, a failure mode encountered and corrected during
development and reported in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}.

Both the random forest and the gradient boosting models were fitted twice,
once to the level of log concentration and once to its change from the
forecast origin, since a tree cannot extrapolate beyond the range of targets
it was trained on and this series drifts across the decade of record;
modelling the change removes that handicap by asking the tree to represent a
roughly stationary residual rather than a trending level.

\section{Deep Learning Methods}
\label{sec:dl-methods}

\subsection{The Gated Recurrent Unit: Architecture and Training}
\label{sec:gru}

The gated recurrent unit \citep{cho2014gru} maintains a hidden state
$h_t \in \mathbb{R}^H$ updated at each timestep $t$ by two gates. The update
gate $z_t$ controls how much of the previous state is retained against how
much is replaced by a new candidate state; the reset gate $r_t$ controls how
much of the previous state is used in forming that candidate:
\begin{align}
z_t &= \sigma\big(W_z x_t + U_z h_{t-1} + b_z\big), \label{eq:gru-z}\\
r_t &= \sigma\big(W_r x_t + U_r h_{t-1} + b_r\big), \label{eq:gru-r}\\
\tilde h_t &= \tanh\big(W_h x_t + U_h (r_t \odot h_{t-1}) + b_h\big), \label{eq:gru-htilde}\\
h_t &= (1-z_t)\odot h_{t-1} \;+\; z_t \odot \tilde h_t, \label{eq:gru-h}
\end{align}
where $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid, $\odot$ is elementwise
multiplication, and $W_z$, $W_r$, $W_h$, $U_z$, $U_r$, $U_h$, $b_z$, $b_r$,
$b_h$ are the parameters
learned by training, fitted by backpropagation through time, the sequential
application of the backpropagation algorithm \citep{rumelhart1986backprop}
across every timestep in the input window. Because the final state $h_t$ in
Equation~\ref{eq:gru-h} is a convex combination of the previous state and the
new candidate rather than a product of many successive nonlinear
transformations, gradients can flow backward through many timesteps without
vanishing in the sense formalised by \citet{bengio1994vanishing}, which is
the property that motivated gated architectures in Section~\ref{sec:lit-dl}.

The specific network fitted in this project is a single GRU layer with
$H=24$ hidden units, reading a sequence of the last 30 days
($t-29,\dots,t$), each day carrying six channels: the logarithm of
concentration, a missingness flag, and two pairs of annual Fourier terms
($K=2$), a smaller harmonic set than the $K=4$ used for the ARIMA
specification in Section~\ref{sec:arima}, inherited from an earlier draft
of the architecture rather than a deliberately tested choice.
Section~\ref{sec:limitations} reports a direct check of $K=4$ for the
network as well, which improves it at every horizon and substantially so
at three days ahead, so the smaller set is better read as an unexamined
default than a justified one. A
linear output layer maps the final hidden state
$h_t$ to a single predicted value, the change in log concentration from the
forecast origin, with the origin value added back afterwards; modelling the
change rather than the level is the same device used for the tree models in
Section~\ref{sec:ml-methods}, for the same reason. The network is trained by
minimising mean absolute error with the Adam optimiser, with early stopping
on a chronological holdout, the most recent 15 per cent of each training
window, so that training stops once validation error no longer improves
rather than at a fixed epoch count.

Writing $d$ for the number of input channels, Equations~\ref{eq:gru-z}
to~\ref{eq:gru-h} fix weight matrices $W_z,W_r,W_h \in \mathbb{R}^{H\times d}$
and $U_z,U_r,U_h \in \mathbb{R}^{H\times H}$ for the three gates, $3H(d+H)$
weights before a single bias is counted. The implementation used here,
PyTorch's \texttt{nn.GRU}, trains each gate's bias as two separately
learned halves rather than the one term $b_z$, $b_r$, $b_h$ that
Equations~\ref{eq:gru-z} to~\ref{eq:gru-h} show, one added to the input
term and one to the hidden term and the two summed inside the gate, a
convention shared with cuDNN-backed implementations generally rather than a
departure from what those equations state. That doubles the bias count the
equations alone would suggest, $6H$ rather than $3H$, giving
\begin{equation}
3H(d+H+2) \;+\; (H+1)
\label{eq:gru-params}
\end{equation}
trainable parameters in total, the second term the linear output layer's
own weight vector and bias. For $H=24$, Equation~\ref{eq:gru-params} gives
2{,}329 parameters for the six-channel network, $d=6$, and 2{,}617 for the
ten-channel weather version, $d=10$, both confirmed directly by counting
the fitted model objects' own parameters rather than trusted as arithmetic.

A recurrent network forces a compromise that no other model in this project
requires. It must be handed a value at every timestep: it cannot skip one the
way the state space model in Section~\ref{sec:arima} skips a measurement
update, and it cannot accept a missing value the way the histogram gradient
boosting model in Section~\ref{sec:ml-methods} can. Gaps are therefore carried
forward in the log-concentration channel, with the separate missingness flag
marking which days were filled rather than observed, the same
forward-fill-plus-indicator construction \citet{che2018rnn} use for
recurrent networks over clinical time series with the same structural gap,
a value required at every timestep and a sensor that does not always
provide one. The one architecture Dr Tian specifically asked to be included
is the one architecture in the suite that cannot represent the statement
that a value is unknown.

A second version of this network reads two further channels, the day's mean
temperature and wind speed from Section~\ref{sec:weather}, each paired with
its own missingness flag in exactly the same construction used for the
concentration channel, ten channels in total rather than six. Wind speed in
particular is a plausible carrier of the short range structure that already
let the plain network beat ARIMA at one day ahead in the negative result
anticipated in Section~\ref{sec:lit-dl}: a calm, stagnant airmass is both the
immediate physical precondition for a particulate episode and a quantity the
Fourier terms, which know only the calendar, cannot represent at all. Results
for both versions are given in Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1}.

Because the network's weights are initialised randomly, its forecast depends
on that initialisation, unlike every other model in this project. It is
therefore fitted independently across ten random seeds, and its result is
reported throughout Chapter~\ref{chap:results} as the range across those
ten runs, never as a single seed's point estimate; the justification for
treating this as a reporting requirement rather than a presentational choice
is given in Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1}. The sample was doubled from an
initial five seeds to ten after rerunning the full pipeline on this same
machine reproduced every classical and tree-based model's score exactly but
moved the network's by nearly as much as the gap between two genuinely
different seeds, evidence that its training is not bit-reproducible even
with \texttt{--seed} fixed; Section~\ref{sec:limitations} returns to what
that means for the results that follow. The architecture itself, $H=24$ and
a 30-day window, was fixed by inspection rather than by the held-out search
used for the tree models' capacity in Section~\ref{sec:ml-methods};
Section~\ref{sec:limitations} also reports a bounded check of that choice,
run after the fact.

\section{Rolling-Origin Evaluation}
\label{sec:rolling}

Every model was evaluated over 2{,}303 origins from 9 November 2019 to 24 August
2026, spanning 6.8 years, with a three year burn-in and model state advanced
daily between refits. Parameters are re-estimated every 90 days for every
specification except the recurrent network, which refits every 180 days:
each of its refits trains a network from scratch rather than solving a
closed form or appending one more observation to an already-converged
filter, so halving its refit frequency is the practical cost of including
it in the suite at all rather than an oversight.

This is not a refinement of a single train-test split; it replaces one, for the
reason standard cross-validation is inappropriate for dependent data in the
first place: shuffling origins lets a model trained on the future score itself
against the past \citep{bergmeir2012crossvalidation}. On a single test block the
ARIMA scored 0.903 in relative terms at one day ahead; under the rolling-origin
harness built to replace it, the same model scores 0.940, worse rather than
better, because the single block happened to be calmer than the training
period and was flattering every model. A single split is one draw from a
process, and a conclusion drawn from it is a conclusion about that period,
exactly the instability in single-split evaluation that \citet{tashman2000outofsample}
documents across decades of applied forecasting studies and that
\citet{hewamalage2023evaluation} report as still common practice. The
rolling-origin design used throughout this project is adopted specifically
to avoid being another instance of the pattern both papers describe.

The governing invariant is that at origin $t$ a model may use observations up to
and including day $t$ and nothing else: not the value at $t+1$, not a parameter
estimated using data after $t$, and not a scaling constant or imputed value
computed from the full series. Since nothing fails visibly when that is broken,
and the numbers merely improve, the invariant is enforced by construction and
tested directly. Every model runs through one shared loop, and that loop is
verified by corrupting the series from a chosen date, rerunning, and requiring
that no forecast issued before that date changes.

One trap is specific to supervised learning under a rolling origin. At origin $t$
the label attached to feature row $t'$ is the concentration at $t' + h$, so the
training set ends at $t - h$ rather than at $t$. A separate model is fitted per
horizon because that arithmetic requires it. The error would have amounted to
three rows per refit and would have been entirely invisible in the output.

\section{Evaluation Measures}
\label{sec:evalmeasures}

Accuracy is reported separately at each horizon and never averaged, since skill
decays with horizon and concealing that would defeat the purpose. Writing
$e_i = \hat y_i - y_i$ for the forecast error of row $i$ among the $n$ rows a
model is scored on, the headline measure is relative mean absolute error
against the persistence forecast, computed on identical rows,
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{rMAE} \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{MAE}(\text{model})}{\mathrm{MAE}(\text{persistence})},
\qquad \mathrm{MAE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|e_i|,
\label{eq:rmae}
\end{equation}
so that 1.000 is persistence and values below one beat it. Mean absolute
scaled error,
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{MASE} \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{MAE}(\text{model})}
{\frac{1}{n_{\text{train}}-1}\sum_{t=2}^{n_{\text{train}}}|y_t - y_{t-1}|},
\label{eq:mase}
\end{equation}
proposed by \citet{hyndman2006mase} as a scale-free
accuracy measure that remains defined even when the series passes through
values near zero, is reported alongside, but its denominator is fixed on the
training period and therefore also reflects any difference in volatility
between training and test periods, which is material here; this is the same
distinction between a scaled error and a relative error that motivated
reporting both rather than either alone.

As a warning system, a day is an event if the observed concentration exceeds the
health threshold, and an alarm is raised when the forecast exceeds a decision
threshold. These are separate quantities and are kept separate throughout.
Every warning-system measure reported is a ratio of four counts accumulated
over the days a model is scored on: true positives $\mathrm{TP}$, an alarm
on an event day; false positives $\mathrm{FP}$, an alarm on a quiet day;
false negatives $\mathrm{FN}$, a missed event; and true negatives
$\mathrm{TN}$, a quiet day correctly left unflagged. Reported are the hit
rate,
\begin{equation}
\text{hit rate} \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN}},
\label{eq:hitrate}
\end{equation}
the share of actual events the model catches; the false alarm rate, defined
as false alarms divided by quiet days rather than by alarms raised,
\begin{equation}
\text{false alarm rate} \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{FP}}{\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{TN}};
\label{eq:farrate}
\end{equation}
precision, the share of alarms that were right,
\begin{equation}
\text{precision} \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}};
\label{eq:precision}
\end{equation}
the critical success index \citep{schaefer1990csi},
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{CSI} \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{FN}},
\label{eq:csi}
\end{equation}
which discards $\mathrm{TN}$ entirely; and alarms raised per year,
$365.25\,(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP})/n$, included because a false alarm rate of
0.10 sounds negligible and means roughly one wasted alarm every ten quiet
days, which is what an operator actually experiences. Plain classification
accuracy, $(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{TN})/n$, is deliberately never reported as a
warning-system measure: with hazardous days a minority class throughout the
record, $\mathrm{TN}$ dominates $n$, so a model that never raises an alarm,
$\mathrm{TP}=\mathrm{FP}=0$, scores $\mathrm{TN}/n$ on accuracy, high by
construction, while catching none of the events it exists to catch
\citep{he2009imbalance}. Equations~\ref{eq:hitrate} to~\ref{eq:csi} are
exactly the decomposition that distortion motivates, a precision-recall-style
reading of the same contingency table rather than a single aggregate rate on
imbalanced data \citep{saito2015prplot}.

\section{Statistical Comparison of Forecasts}
\label{sec:dmtest}

Section~\ref{sec:noise-floor} bounds how large a gap between two models'
scores must be before it is more than measurement noise, but that bound is
empirical: it is the amount a score moved when nothing about the model or
the data changed, not a sampling distribution with a $p$-value attached.
The Diebold-Mariano test \citep{diebold1995predictive} supplies the formal
version of the same question. For two models with forecast errors $e_{1,t}$
and $e_{2,t}$ at the same horizon $h$ and the same forecast origins, define
the loss differential
\begin{equation}
d_t \;=\; L(e_{1,t}) \;-\; L(e_{2,t}),
\label{eq:dm-diff}
\end{equation}
with $L(e) = |e|$ throughout, matching this report's own headline measure,
Equation~\ref{eq:rmae}, rather than squared error. Under the null hypothesis
of equal predictive accuracy, $E[d_t] = 0$, and the test statistic is
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{DM} \;=\; \frac{\bar d}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\bar d)}},
\qquad \bar d = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n} d_t,
\label{eq:dm-stat}
\end{equation}
asymptotically standard normal under the null. The variance estimate is not
the plain sample variance divided by $n$: an optimally specified $h$-step
forecast has errors that are at most an $\mathrm{MA}(h-1)$ process, so the
loss differential it produces carries genuine serial correlation up to lag
$h-1$, which Diebold and Mariano's derivation folds into a long-run
variance,
\begin{equation}
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\bar d) \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\left[\hat\gamma_0 \;+\;
2\sum_{k=1}^{h-1}\hat\gamma_k\right], \qquad
\hat\gamma_k \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=k+1}^{n}(d_t-\bar d)(d_{t-k}-\bar d),
\label{eq:dm-var}
\end{equation}
rather than the plain estimator a reader more familiar with an ordinary
paired $t$-test might expect; at $h=1$ there is nothing to correct for and
Equation~\ref{eq:dm-var} reduces to the ordinary case, $\hat\gamma_0/n$.
Because this project's longest horizon is three days, the correction is
never more than two autocovariance terms. The asymptotic normal
approximation can be anti-conservative at the sample sizes forecasting
studies actually have, so this report uses the small-sample correction of
\citet{harvey1997dmtest},
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{DM}^{*} \;=\; \mathrm{DM}\left[\frac{n+1-2h+h(h-1)/n}{n}\right]^{1/2},
\label{eq:dm-hln}
\end{equation}
referred to a $t_{n-1}$ distribution rather than the standard normal, which
is uniformly more conservative and is what every statistic and $p$-value
attributed to this test in Chapter~\ref{chap:results} actually uses.
That correction addresses the sample size directly, but the asymptotic
justification behind both the uncorrected and the corrected statistic
still rests on a central limit theorem applying to $\bar d$, and this
report has shown PM2.5 itself to be strongly right skewed with
occasional extreme episodes: a loss differential built from absolute
errors on that scale can inherit some of the same heavy-tailedness, which
is exactly the condition under which a normal approximation converges
more slowly. Nothing in Chapter~\ref{chap:results} checks this directly,
for instance by bootstrapping the statistic's own sampling distribution
rather than relying on the asymptotic one; the correction applied here
addresses a known and specific failure mode of the test, not every way
its normal approximation could be imprecise on a series with this one's
particular shape.

This is applied to exactly the comparison Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1}
already makes by counting seed signs against the empirical noise floor: the
recurrent network against the ARIMA benchmark, with and without weather, at
every horizon. Because the network alone depends on a random
initialisation, the test is run once per seed against the same ARIMA
forecast and reported as the range across all ten, exactly the convention
already used for every other seed-dependent number in this report, rather
than as a single run's $p$-value that a different seed could have produced
differently.

\section{Reproducibility}

The analysis runs end to end from an empty directory via ten numbered
pipeline scripts, nine of which carry an automated correctness test, run
with \texttt{--test}, that exits before producing any output if its own
checks fail. The rolling origin harness verifies its own leakage
invariant before every run. Every table in this report is generated directly
from the result files by \texttt{make\_tables.py}; no number has been
transcribed by hand. Raw and cleaned data are held under version control so
that the analysis does not depend on the data provider serving identical
values at a later date, which the finding in Section~\ref{sec:data} suggests
is not a safe assumption. The complete repository, including every commit
from initial data acquisition to this report, is public and runnable at
\texttt{github.com/JC16092/mth5000-aqi-forecast}.

\section{Chapter Summary}

This chapter described the data, two defects found in it, and the feature
table built from it, including an optional weather extension
(Section~\ref{sec:weather}) carrying its own third data-quality defect, a
hard cutoff rather than scattered gaps, and then gave the full mathematical
specification of the two method families compared in this project. Machine learning, in
Section~\ref{sec:ml-methods}, comprises a classical ARIMA benchmark and three
regressors, ridge, random forest, and gradient boosting, each controlling
the bias-variance trade-off by a different mechanism: shrinkage, bagging, or
additive stagewise correction. Deep learning, in Section~\ref{sec:dl-methods},
comprises a single gated recurrent network, whose gating mechanism is
specifically what lets it avoid the vanishing-gradient failure of a plain
recurrent network. Every model is evaluated under the same rolling-origin
protocol, specified in Section~\ref{sec:rolling}, and scored by the same
measures, specified in Section~\ref{sec:evalmeasures}, so that the comparison
in Chapter~\ref{chap:results} is a fair one; where that comparison involves
the network against the ARIMA benchmark, it is also given a formal
significance test, specified in Section~\ref{sec:dmtest}.
