Table~\ref{tab:accuracy} and Figure~\ref{fig:accuracy} answer the first
research question, and the answer is not uniform across horizons.

At one day ahead the recurrent network is the best model, and this is robust:
across ten initialisation seeds it is numerically ahead of the ARIMA
specification in every one, and clearly so, beyond this report's own 0.004
noise floor (Section~\ref{sec:noise-floor}), in eight of the ten; the two
weakest, 0.936 and 0.939 against ARIMA's 0.940, are close enough to call
ties rather than clear wins. At two days the picture is closer: ARIMA is
numerically ahead in nine of the ten seeds, but only five of those nine
clear the noise floor, one seed (0.878) beats ARIMA outright, and the
remaining four are indistinguishable from it. At three days neither model
has a seed that clears the floor against the other: the best network seed,
0.831, and ARIMA's 0.832 are separated by a few parts in ten thousand, a tie
in any language that would survive examination, while the worst network
seed, 0.879, is clearly the weaker of the two.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Diebold-Mariano test of the recurrent network against the ARIMA
benchmark (Section~\ref{sec:dmtest}), run once per seed and given as the
range across all ten. A negative statistic favours the network at that
seed; a positive one favours ARIMA. The last column counts seeds reaching
$p<0.05$, two-sided.}
\label{tab:significance}
\input{tables/significance}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:significance} puts a formal test behind the comparison the
paragraph above makes by counting seed signs against an empirical floor. At
one day ahead the statistic favours the network in all ten seeds and the
advantage reaches $p<0.05$ in four of them. At two days, every seed's
$p$-value exceeds 0.07 and none reaches significance. At three days exactly
one seed does, and in ARIMA's favour, $p=0.0056$; the rest do not.
Section~\ref{sec:noise-floor} returns to this table directly, since it asks
the same question the empirical noise floor does and answers it more
conservatively at every horizon reported there.

The mechanism is only partly architectural. At one day ahead the forecast is
dominated by short-range structure, where a nonlinear model has something to
exploit. As the horizon lengthens the seasonal component takes over, and
ARIMA's four Fourier pairs carry more of it than the network's two
(Section~\ref{sec:gru}), not because the network lacks an explicit seasonal
signal altogether but because it receives a coarser one.
Section~\ref{sec:limitations} reports a bounded check of exactly that
difference, and it accounts for a meaningful share of the gap at three days.

The network is reported as a range rather than a point because it is the only
model whose result depends on a random initialisation, and the dependence is not
small. Across ten seeds the spread is 0.029 at one day, 0.028 at two and 0.048 at
three. At three days that spread is wider than the gap separating the ARIMA from
two of the other models in the table, so a single seed could have been reported
as beating them or losing to them at the analyst's convenience.

Two subsidiary results support the specification choices. Removing the Fourier
terms from the ARIMA degrades it by 3.3 points of relative error at one day and
by 5.8 points at three, under the same rolling-origin harness, so the seasonal
terms earn their place and increasingly so with horizon. Modelling the change
from the origin rather than the level improves
both tree models, because a tree cannot extrapolate beyond the targets it was
trained on and this series drifts downward across the decade.

Table~\ref{tab:significance} tests only the one comparison in this report
with a seed to range over. The same test applies just as directly to the
other four machine learning regressors against ARIMA: each is reported as
a single fit rather than a range, so one Diebold-Mariano statistic per
horizon is the whole comparison, not an average over several.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Diebold-Mariano test of ARIMA against each point-forecast machine
learning regressor (Section~\ref{sec:dmtest}). A negative statistic favours
the machine learning model; a positive one favours ARIMA. An asterisk marks
$p<0.05$, two-sided.}
\label{tab:significance-ml}
\footnotesize
\input{tables/significance_ml}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:significance-ml} backs the chapter's other central claim,
that the classical benchmark beats every machine learning regressor at
every horizon, with the same kind of formal test already given to the
network comparison, rather than leaving it to point estimates and the
informal noise floor alone. The statistic favours ARIMA in all fifteen
model-horizon pairings, and fourteen reach $p<0.05$; the one exception,
the change-target random forest at two days, falls just short at
$p=0.054$. This is, if anything, a stronger formal result than the
network comparison can supply for its own horizons, precisely because
none of these four regressors carries a seed's worth of sampling
uncertainty on top of the test's own.

\subsection{Does Weather Change the Answer?}
\label{sec:results-weather}

The specification above uses no information beyond the series' own history.
Section~\ref{sec:weather} adds daily wind speed and temperature, and the
question is whether that changes which model wins.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Change in rMAE from adding weather covariates, same rolling-origin
protocol and same reference as Table~\ref{tab:accuracy}. Negative is an
improvement. The network's weather row is given as its own absolute range
over ten seeds, to be read against its row in Table~\ref{tab:accuracy}.}
\label{tab:weather}
\footnotesize
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{tables/weather}}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:weather} answers it unevenly across models, and the unevenness
is itself informative. Gradient boosting improves substantially and at every
horizon, by 8.2 points of relative error at one day, 2.0 at two and 2.9 at
three on the level target, and similarly on the change target. The random
forest moves the other way at the longest horizon, 5.3 points worse at three
days, while ridge improves at one and two days and worsens slightly at three.
No single story explains all five machine learning rows; weather is not a
free improvement for every method that can accept it.

The recurrent network is where the extension matters most, because
Section~\ref{sec:weather} identified wind speed as a specific physical
candidate for the short range structure the plain network was already
exploiting at one day ahead. With weather added, the network beats ARIMA
clearly under all ten seeds at one day ahead, as before. At two days, where
ARIMA previously won outright, the picture becomes a genuine contest rather
than a clean win for either side: three of ten seeds beat ARIMA clearly,
beyond the 0.004 noise floor established in Section~\ref{sec:noise-floor},
six are indistinguishable from it within that floor, and one is a clear
loss. At three days a similar three-way split appears with different seeds
in each role: three of ten beat ARIMA clearly, two are ties, and five, a
majority, are clear losses, including one seed 0.041 worse than ARIMA.
Doubling the seed count from the five first fitted is what surfaced this;
under the first five alone, both horizons had looked like a win for the
network, and that reading did not survive a second, independent batch of
five seeds.

The same formal test behind Table~\ref{tab:significance} reaches a similar
verdict for the weather version, in its lower block. At one day ahead it
favours the network in all ten seeds and reaches $p<0.05$ in seven, a
stronger formal result than the plain network's four, consistent with wind
speed carrying genuine short-range information rather than noise that a
larger input simply fits more closely. At two days the direction itself
splits, six seeds favour the network and four favour ARIMA, and not one
seed on either side reaches significance; by this reading the three-way
split the seed-counting above reports is closer to no detectable difference
at all than to a genuine three-way contest. At three days one seed reaches
significance, $p=0.049$, and it favours ARIMA, consistent with the
majority-loss reading above, though a $p$-value that close to the threshold
means a single further seed could move the count either way.

The honest summary is that wind speed and temperature measurably help the
one architecture built to exploit short-range structure at one day ahead,
leave the two-day comparison a genuine tie rather than the win it first
appeared to be, and leave three days ahead more often a loss than a win for
the network, while helping the tree-based machine learning models unevenly
and the random forest not at all at the longest horizon. This was checked
against the weather coverage gap diagnosed in Section~\ref{sec:weather} by
repeating the comparison restricted to origins inside the fully observed
weather window; the ordering at one day ahead survived that restriction, and
so did the mixed, seed-dependent picture at two and three days, which is
what makes the finding a property of the weather signal and of the
network's own training instability, rather than of how the coverage gap was
filled.

That accuracy gain was then carried through to Research Question 3 directly,
by rerunning the threshold sweep from Section~\ref{sec:threshold} with the
weather models added to the roster of candidates at every budget, on exactly
the same rows the accuracy comparison above used.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Best achievable hit rate within an alarm budget, before and after
adding the weather models as candidates, averaged over the five network
seeds. The two rows at each horizon are scored on identical origins; the
only difference is which models are allowed to be the best one.}
\label{tab:weatherbudget}
\footnotesize
\input{tables/weather_budget}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:weatherbudget} gives the answer, and it favours the ceiling
over the gain. At several budgets the weather models do not even supply the
best option, delta exactly zero: 60 alarms a year at one day ahead; 60, 80
and 100 at two; and 40, 80 and 100 at three. Where they do win, the
improvement is small: at most 1.2 points of hit rate, at two days and a
budget of 40, and one point or under at every other budget where they help
at all. That is well below the five-point spread across models documented in
Table~\ref{tab:budget} and discussed in Section~\ref{sec:noise-floor}, not a
new tier above it, and nowhere near the fifty-point range that moving the
budget itself buys. A substantially more accurate point forecast, 8.2 points
of relative error at one day ahead for gradient boosting, translates into at
most a little over a point of additional hit rate once it is run through a
decision threshold. The ceiling this report's central finding describes is not a
property of the ten original models being insufficiently accurate; it
persists even after a materially more accurate forecaster is added to the
comparison.

\section{Two Arms of the Same Question}
\label{sec:arms}

The second research question asks whether it is better to forecast the
concentration and then apply a decision threshold, or to train a classifier
on the exceedance label directly. Comparing the two arms by their single
best model would be misleading, since the forecast-then-threshold arm has
seven regressors to choose from at every budget and the classification arm
has three; the better-resourced arm would look stronger for that reason
alone, regardless of which strategy is actually better. The comparison
below instead matches each classifier to the regressor built from the same
underlying algorithm, ridge against the penalised logistic it most closely
resembles, and the change-target random forest and gradient boosting
models against their own classifier counterparts, so that training
objective is the only thing that varies.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Forecast-then-threshold against direct classification, matched by
base algorithm, at one day ahead. Higher is better; bold marks the better
arm in each column.}
\label{tab:arms}
\footnotesize
\input{tables/arms}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:arms} already shows more structure than a coin flip. Across
all three matched pairs, every horizon, and all four alarm budgets, 36
comparisons in total, forecast-then-threshold wins 21, direct
classification wins 11, and four are exact ties. That is not the even
split a genuinely arbitrary choice would produce, but the margin each time
is almost always small: a median difference of 0.011 in hit rate, and a
largest difference, across every comparison run, of 0.056. Forecasting the
concentration and then thresholding it has a real, modest edge that shrinks
steadily as the alarm budget loosens: it wins 8 of 9 comparisons at a
budget of 40 and 7 of 9 at 60, but direct classification overtakes it at
the loosest budget this report considers, winning 6 of 9 at 100. The edge
is also uneven by horizon, narrowing steadily rather than changing hands:
forecast-then-threshold wins 8 of 12 matched comparisons at one day ahead,
7 of 12 at two days, and 6 of 12 at three. There is no horizon or budget
regime in which direct classification leads at one day or two; it only
overtakes once the alarm budget is loose enough that a classifier's extra
structure stops mattering.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig7_arms}
\caption{Table~\ref{tab:arms} extended to all three horizons: the hit-rate
advantage of forecast-then-threshold over its matched classifier, by alarm
budget, one line per matched pair. Above the zero line forecast-then-
threshold wins; below it the classifier does. The lines start mostly above
zero at a budget of 40 and drift toward it, and below it, as the budget
loosens and the horizon lengthens, the same narrowing the text above
describes as counts rather than as a curve.}
\label{fig:arms}
\end{figure}

A plausible reading is that a classifier optimises the exceedance label
directly and so should have the advantage, while a regressor optimises a
different quantity, squared or absolute error on the concentration, and
only inherits its warning-system performance as a side effect of being
thresholded well. Table~\ref{tab:arms} suggests that advantage is not
realised in practice on a series this size: a classifier trained on roughly
the same few thousand rows has little more signal to find in the label
than a regressor already has in the continuous value, and the regressor's
continuous output carries more information into the threshold sweep than a
single probability does, which may be what the small but consistent edge
reflects.

Given a modest result rather than a decisive one, the forecast-then-threshold
arm is preferred on grounds beyond the numbers in Table~\ref{tab:arms} as
well: it produces a concentration, which can be rethresholded for any future
health policy without refitting, whereas a classifier is bound to the
threshold it was trained on. Both considerations point the same way, which
is why this report's own warning-system results elsewhere, including
Table~\ref{tab:budget} and the weather comparison in
Section~\ref{sec:results-weather}, are built on the forecast-then-threshold
arm throughout rather than on the classifiers.

\section{The Decision Threshold}
\label{sec:threshold}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Best hit rate available within a budget of alarms per year, with the
event fixed at the health threshold and only the decision threshold varying.}
\label{tab:budget}
\footnotesize
\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}{\input{tables/budget}}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:budget} contains the principal result of this project. Moving the
alarm budget from 40 to 100 per year changes the achievable hit rate at one day
ahead from 0.379 to 0.881. Holding the budget fixed and changing the model
instead moves it by around five points.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig5_warning}
\caption{The trade-off, by horizon. The top row shows hit rate against false
alarm rate; the bottom row replaces the false alarm rate with alarms raised per
year, the unit in which an operator budgets. The curves very nearly coincide,
which is the finding. They have deliberately not been separated for legibility.}
\label{fig:warning}
\end{figure}

Two individual comparisons make the point sharper than the aggregate does. At
three days ahead and a budget of 40 alarms a year, persistence, a forecast
that does nothing but repeat yesterday's reading, is not merely competitive
but is the single best model in the entire study, 0.359, ahead of every
machine learning regressor, ARIMA, and every one of the recurrent network's
ten seeds. At the loosest budget this report considers, 100 alarms a year,
and the same horizon, a climatological forecast, which uses no recent
information whatever, comes within roughly a hundredth of the best fitted
model, 0.816 against 0.827.
Figure~\ref{fig:warning} shows the same result as curves; they very nearly
coincide, and they have deliberately not been separated for legibility.

The mechanism behind the first of those two comparisons is already visible
in Figure~\ref{fig:series}: exceedances arrive as multi-day episodes, not
isolated days, so the most informative fact about whether day $t+3$ is
hazardous is often simply that day $t$ already is. Persistence is exactly
the forecast that encodes this and nothing else, carrying today's reading
forward unchanged to every horizon. At a budget this tight, a model may
only raise the alarm on the days its own forecast ranks highest, and the
safest such day to flag is not the onset of a new episode, which nothing in
this suite predicts reliably three days out, but a day already deep inside
one, where persistence's assumption of no change is closest to true. The
more elaborate models are not wrong to forecast a trajectory rather than a
constant; at three days ahead that trajectory is carried mainly by the same
seasonal and autoregressive structure persistence ignores entirely, and
fitting it introduces exactly the small deviations that can cost a model
its place once only the forty most confident days in the whole study are
allowed to count.

The reading is not that modelling is pointless. It is that the quantity a
decision maker controls, namely how many alarms per year can be justified,
dominates the quantity a modeller controls. A report that presents a model
comparison without stating the operating point it was evaluated at has answered a
question nobody asked.

\section{Chapter Summary}

Table~\ref{tab:accuracy} answers the first research question with a
horizon-dependent result: the deep learning model wins at one day ahead, the
classical model wins or ties beyond it. Table~\ref{tab:weather}
(Section~\ref{sec:results-weather}) shows that boundary holding at one day
ahead once observed weather is added, but across ten seeds rather than the
original five it leaves two and three days ahead a statistical tie rather
than a clean win for either model. Carried through to the decision
threshold, Table~\ref{tab:weatherbudget} shows that gain buys only a little
over a point of hit rate at a fixed alarm budget at most, confirming rather
than complicating the answer to the third question.
Table~\ref{tab:arms} (Section~\ref{sec:arms}) answers the second: matched by
algorithm rather than by whichever model happens to be best, forecasting the
concentration and then thresholding it beats direct classification in 21 of
36 comparisons to 11, with four ties, a real but modest edge rather than a
decisive one.
Section~\ref{sec:threshold} answers
the third, and it is the result the rest of this report is organised around:
the alarm budget, not the model, is what principally determines warning
performance. Chapter~\ref{chap:discussion} takes up what that means in
practice.

% ============================================================================
\chapter{Discussion}
\label{chap:discussion}

\section{The Operational Question Dominates the Modelling Question}

Table~\ref{tab:budget} and Figure~\ref{fig:warning} together make a single
point, and this section states what follows from it rather than repeating the
numbers. A decision maker who fixes how many alarms per year an operator or
the public will tolerate has more influence over how many hazardous days are
caught than a modeller choosing among the ten specifications fitted in this
project. Moving the budget from 40 to 100 alarms a year moves the achievable
hit rate at one day ahead from 0.379 to 0.881, a range of fifty points.
Holding the budget fixed and switching the model instead moves the hit rate by
about five points, and at three days ahead, at the loosest budget this report
considers, a climatology forecast that uses no recent information whatever
comes within roughly a hundredth of the best fitted model, 0.816 against 0.827.

This is not an argument against modelling. ARIMA and the recurrent network
both earn real, if modest, gains over persistence in Table~\ref{tab:accuracy},
and a better point forecast still narrows the range of thresholds worth
considering. It is an argument about where the leverage in this problem
actually sits. A hazardous air quality warning system is not a machine
learning benchmark with a threshold attached to it afterwards; the threshold
is the policy instrument, and the forecasting model only supplies its input.
A comparison of models that does not first fix the alarm budget it was
evaluated at has answered a question nobody who has to operate the system
actually asked. The practical recommendation that follows is to treat the
alarm budget as the primary subject of discussion with the health authority
commissioning such a system, and the choice of forecasting model as a
secondary refinement of a curve whose shape is already mostly fixed by what
every model in this study shares: the persistence of concentration from one
day to the next, and the annual cycle.

\section{How Large Is a Difference Between Models?}
\label{sec:noise-floor}

Three results in this project bound that question from below. Running the
identical pipeline on two different machines moved the tree models by up to
0.004 in relative error, because histogram gradient boosting parallelises
with OpenMP and floating point summation order depends on the thread count.
Changing only the random initialisation of the recurrent network moved it by
0.028 to 0.048 across ten seeds. A third and less expected result bounds it
further: rerunning the identical command with the same seed on the same
machine moved the network's score by nearly as much as switching to a
genuinely different seed does, which Section~\ref{sec:limitations} discusses
and which this report takes as the practical floor on how precisely the
network's result can be stated at all.

Table~\ref{tab:accuracy} contains several gaps at or below those two floors, and
naming them is more convincing than asserting that they exist. At one day ahead,
gradient boosting on the change target scores 0.983 and the random forest on the
level target scores 0.988, a gap of 0.004, right at the floor measured on a
different model entirely. The same pair sits even closer together at three
days, 0.878 against 0.879, a gap of 0.001, well inside that floor rather than
merely at it. Neither pair can be ordered with any confidence given a floor
measured at that same size on a different model entirely; the measurement was
never repeated for every pair in the table, so the honest reading is that it
might apply more broadly than the one architecture it was taken on, not that
it is known to be absent elsewhere.

The sharpest instance involves the recurrent network directly, because its own
reported range is wide enough to supply the comparison by itself. At three days
ahead, the network's worst seed scores 0.879, a thousandth away from gradient
boosting's change-target result of 0.878, several rows lower in the same
table. Nothing about the data or the method changed between those
two numbers; a different random seed for the one architecture that has one was
enough to move it from a result indistinguishable from the classical benchmark,
at that same horizon the network's best seed ties ARIMA to within a few parts
in ten thousand (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1}), to one indistinguishable from
the weakest-looking machine learning regressor in the table. A table that printed only one of those two seeds would have told a reader
something true about that run and nothing reliable about the architecture.

Several of the gaps between adjacent models in Table~\ref{tab:accuracy} are of
that order even where no seed or machine-level floor was measured directly for
that pair. Any claim that one of those models is better than another, made
without stating the run to run variation, is not supported by the evidence.

A formal test of the same question, rather than a tolerance measured by
rerunning and compared by eye, is available for the one comparison in this
report with enough seeds to support it: the network against ARIMA, in
Table~\ref{tab:significance} (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1}). It is,
throughout, the more conservative reading. At one day ahead the network's
advantage reaches conventional significance in four of the ten seeds, not
the eight credited to it by the noise-floor count above; at two days none
of the ten reaches it, where the noise-floor count had already read most of
the table as a tie; at three days a single seed does, and even that one
only at $p=0.049$. The two readings differ because each bounds something
different. The noise floor measured here, 0.004 to 0.048, bounds how much a
score moves for reasons that have nothing to do with which model is better:
thread scheduling, floating point summation order, a different draw of
initial weights. The Diebold-Mariano statistic bounds something else
entirely, how much the mean of a loss differential computed over roughly
1{,}700 individually autocorrelated daily forecast errors can vary by
chance even when the two models being compared are, in truth, equally
good. Both are genuine sources of uncertainty in a result this report
already reports as a range rather than a point; the formal test shows the
second is generally the larger of the two in this project, which is a
reason to read Table~\ref{tab:accuracy}'s gaps even more cautiously than the
noise floor alone suggests, not a reason to discard the noise floor in
favour of the test. The noise floor is measured directly from reruns,
where the Diebold-Mariano variance estimate in Equation~\ref{eq:dm-var} is
necessarily a model of the error process rather than a direct measurement
of it; a result that failed either bound on its own would be the one
actually worth re-examining.

One more layer of uncertainty sits on top of both readings: the seed
counts themselves are small-sample proportions, not settled facts. Four
of ten seeds reaching significance at one day ahead is itself a point
estimate with a wide interval; a Wilson score interval on that proportion
runs from 0.17 to 0.69 at the conventional 95\% level, and the
all-or-nothing counts at two and three days, 0 of 10 and 1 of 10, carry
intervals of their own, up to 0.28 and 0.40 respectively. A different
batch of ten seeds could plausibly have produced a noticeably different
count at any horizon without the underlying comparison having changed at
all. This is not a reason to distrust the direction of any of the three
findings, which the formal test, the noise floor and the point estimates
all agree on, but it is a reason not to treat the exact fraction reported
at each horizon as more precise than the sample it was counted from
allows.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

The analysis rests on a single monitor, OpenAQ location 8118, which
Section~\ref{sec:data} shows is supplied through AirNow and is almost
certainly a United States diplomatic post instrument rather than a station in
the Central Pollution Control Board network. It was chosen because it is the
only nearby monitor with a complete decade of record, against the eighteen
months every CPCB station returns; the choice buys history at the cost of
representativeness. The absence of a weekly cycle documented in
Section~\ref{sec:weekly} is consistent with a diplomatic enclave rather than a
roadside site, which supports this reading of the limitation rather than
leaving it an unrelated coincidence, but it does not change the fact that
every number in this report describes one point in the city rather than Delhi
as a whole.

The project forecasts one city. Delhi was chosen because its air quality
problem is severe and well documented, not because it is representative of
Indian cities generally. Pollution sources, meteorology, and the strength of
the seasonal cycle that drives the Fourier terms in Section~\ref{sec:weekly}
all vary by region, and a coastal city or one without a dominant biomass
burning season could show a different balance between the classical and
machine learning models, or a genuine weekly cycle where this station shows
none. Nothing in this report should be read as a claim about any station or
city other than the one it was fitted to.

The upper cleaning threshold of 1000\,\textmu g\,m$^{-3}$ is a judgement rather
than a fact, and its effect on the reported conclusions was checked directly
rather than assumed. Restoring the seven days it removes, including the three
identical readings at 1990 diagnosed in Section~\ref{sec:defects} as a clipped
instrument ceiling, gives 3{,}100 usable days and 927 exceedance days rather
than 3{,}093 and 920, a small shift. Refitting the full rolling-origin harness
on this uncapped series leaves the ARIMA specification essentially unchanged,
0.935 against 0.940 at one day ahead and 0.829 against 0.832 at three days,
because working in logarithms and differencing the series absorbs the
contamination. The machine learning models are not so protected. Ridge moves
from a near tie with persistence to a clear loss at one day ahead, 0.997 to
1.118, and gradient boosting on the level target moves from a narrow win over
persistence to a loss at three days, 0.883 to 1.006. The central finding of
Research Question 1, that the classical benchmark beats every machine learning
model at every horizon, therefore does not merely survive removing the
threshold; it strengthens, because the models it beat most narrowly are
precisely the ones most exposed to the uncleaned tail. The threshold matters,
but it matters more to the machine learning suite than to the model this
project ultimately recommends.

Hyperparameters for the tree-based models were chosen at every refit from a
small explicit grid, scored on a held-out slice of the training window taken
in time order, rather than from an exhaustive or Bayesian search. This
followed a real failure during development, in which fixed hyperparameters let
gradient boosting overfit badly enough to score worse than persistence; the
grid search fixed that specific problem, but a small grid can still miss a
configuration that a wider search would find. The machine learning results in
Table~\ref{tab:accuracy} should therefore be read as a lower bound on what
those model classes could achieve with more computation, not as their ceiling.

The recurrent network's own architecture, 24 hidden units and a 30-day
input window, was fixed by inspection, with no search equivalent to the
tree models' grid. A bounded check run after the fact, fitting once on
the original training/validation split used before the rolling-origin
harness existed rather than refitting the full ten-seed evaluation, varied
hidden size and window length one at a time across six settings and three
of the ten seeds used elsewhere. At one day ahead the default is within
0.2 points of relative error of the best setting tried, a longer window;
at two days it is the best of the six outright. At three days, the
horizon where the classical benchmark already has the clearest edge, the
default is the worst of the six: a 45-day window scored 2.2 points better
on this check. Whether that gap would survive the full rolling-origin
evaluation across all ten seeds is untested, and nothing in
Table~\ref{tab:accuracy} has been changed on the strength of a
single-split, three-seed result. The honest reading is that the three-day
comparison in this report rests on a configuration this check found a
clearly better alternative to, while the one- and two-day comparisons
rest on a configuration at or near the best of those tried.

The same bounded method applied to a different setting: holding hidden
size and window length at the report's defaults and varying only the
number of Fourier harmonics the network receives, from the two pairs used
throughout this report to the four ARIMA uses, on the same single-split
check and the same three seeds. At one day ahead the difference is
negligible, an improvement of 0.07 points. At two days, four harmonics
improve the mean by 0.55 points. At three days, the horizon where ARIMA's
advantage is otherwise clearest, four harmonics improve the mean by 3.96
points: low enough on this check that the network's mean would sit
numerically below ARIMA's reported rolling-origin figure, not above it.
This does not show that the ten-seed rolling-origin result at three days
would change if the network were refit with four harmonics there too;
that run was not done, and a gap this size on one validation split is not
automatically the same gap under the full evaluation. It does show that
the account above of why ARIMA wins at longer horizons, that the network
has to learn seasonality a classical model is simply handed, is not quite
right: the network is handed a coarser version of the same signal, and how
much of the gap that coarseness explains, as opposed to a genuine
representational limit, is now an open and fairly pointed question rather
than a closed one.

A full rerun of this project's pipeline, performed late in the writing
process specifically to refresh every result from scratch, surfaced a
further limitation worth stating plainly rather than leaving implicit in a
table footnote. Every classical and tree-based model reproduced its
reported score either exactly (ARIMA, ridge, the benchmarks) or within a
few thousandths (random forest, gradient boosting) when refitted on the
same machine with the same fixed random seeds. The recurrent network did
not: rerunning the identical command with the same \texttt{--seed} moved
its score by nearly as much as switching to a genuinely different seed
does, evidently because training accumulates small floating-point
differences from multi-threaded linear algebra over many epochs in a way a
single tree fit does not. The practical consequence is that five seeds,
this project's original sample, was not enough to characterise the network
reliably: the weather-covariate finding at two and three days ahead
(Section~\ref{sec:results-weather}) looked like a clear win under the
first five seeds fitted and looked like a tie or a loss once five more were
added. The sample was doubled to ten seeds throughout this report for that
reason, and even ten should be read as a reduction in the problem rather
than a solution to it; a result reported as a range across seeds is a
statement about the spread of outcomes this training procedure produces,
not a bound on where its true performance lies.

Wind speed and temperature were added, in Section~\ref{sec:weather}, but the
treatment is narrower than a full meteorological extension in two specific
ways that should be stated plainly rather than discovered by a careful
reader. First, only observed weather enters the feature table, never a
forecast one; a real early-warning system would feed in a numerical weather
prediction for the days ahead, which is a materially stronger and untested
claim about what is knowable at the forecast origin. Second, boundary layer
height, the variable most directly tied to the physical mechanism of a
particulate episode, a shallow boundary layer trapping pollutants near the
surface, is not available from \texttt{meteostat} at all; it would need a
reanalysis product such as ERA5, a separate data acquisition problem rather
than the free extension this report's own earlier draft assumed it would be.
What was carried through, in Section~\ref{sec:results-weather}, is the
threshold sweep: the accuracy gain from weather survives contact with the
decision threshold only partially, buying a few points of hit rate at some
budgets and none at others, which is itself the clearer instance of this
report's central finding rather than a loose end.

\section{Chapter Summary}

Section~\ref{sec:threshold} (Chapter~\ref{chap:results}) established that the
alarm budget dominates the model; this chapter has argued why that is not an
argument against modelling, and has tried to be as honest about the limits of
the modelling itself as about its result. Section~\ref{sec:noise-floor} showed
that several of the gaps in Table~\ref{tab:accuracy} are no larger than noise
this project measured directly, so a horizon-by-horizon ranking read off that
table without the floor in mind would overstate what is known. The
Limitations above add to that the single-station and single-city scope, a
cleaning threshold that is a judgement rather than a fact, hyperparameter
grids that were never exhaustively searched, a weather extension narrower
than a full meteorological system, and a recurrent network whose training is
not bit-reproducible even at a fixed seed, discovered only because the
pipeline was rerun and the result checked rather than assumed. None of these
overturns the central finding; several of them, the noise floor and the
seed-count doubling most directly, are the reason that finding can be stated
with the confidence it is.

% ============================================================================
\chapter{Conclusion}
\label{chap:conclusion}

\section{Summary of the Study}

This project forecast hazardous PM2.5 days at a single Delhi monitor one to
three days ahead, comparing a classical benchmark against three machine
learning regressors and a deep recurrent network, and evaluating every
specification as a warning system rather than by average error alone. Two
real defects in the source data, a clipped instrument ceiling and a
mischaracterised coverage statistic, were found and corrected before any
model was fitted, and an assumption carried over from the approved proposal,
that the series holds a weekly cycle alongside its annual one, was tested
directly and found false.

\section{Main Conclusions}

Across ten models spanning simple benchmarks, a classical time series model,
four machine learning regressors, and a recurrent network, the spread in
achievable hit rate at a fixed alarm budget is about five percentage points;
the spread across alarm budgets, holding the model fixed, is about fifty. The
choice a decision maker makes about how many alarms per year can be
justified therefore has far more influence on how many hazardous days are
caught than the choice a modeller makes among the specifications fitted
here.

Machine learning earned its place only partially. ARIMA with annual Fourier
terms beats every machine learning regressor at every horizon, now backed by
a Diebold-Mariano test at every one of those comparisons rather than point
estimates alone (Section~\ref{sec:results-rq1}), a result that strengthens
rather than weakens under the sensitivity analysis in
Section~\ref{sec:limitations}. Among models using the series' own history
alone, the recurrent network is the one that wins, and only at one day ahead,
reported honestly as a range across ten random initialisations rather than
as a single favourable seed. Adding wind speed and temperature
(Section~\ref{sec:results-weather}) does not move that boundary as cleanly
as a first batch of five seeds suggested: across ten seeds the
weather-enabled network still wins clearly at one day ahead, but at two
days it is tied with ARIMA within this report's own noise floor for six of
ten seeds and ahead for only three, and at three days it is more often a
clear loss than a win, five of ten against three. Doubling the seed count
is what surfaced this, and Section~\ref{sec:limitations} discusses why the
network's training is the one part of this project's methodology where a
fixed seed does not guarantee a fixed answer. Gradient boosting improves at
every horizon with the same weather covariates, though the random forest
does not, so the gain is specific to which model and which architecture,
not a blanket effect of adding more inputs. Carried through the decision
threshold, that accuracy gain buys at most a little over a point of hit
rate at a fixed alarm budget and nothing at all at most of them, which is
this report's central finding recurring at a more demanding test: even a
forecaster that looked materially more accurate under an initial, smaller
sample does not escape the ceiling the alarm budget imposes.

On the second research question, forecasting the concentration and then
thresholding it beats training a classifier directly on the exceedance
label, but only modestly: matched by algorithm rather than by whichever
model happens to be best, it wins 21 of 36 comparisons to 11, with four
ties, a real lean rather than the coin flip a single qualitative judgement
would suggest, yet still small enough in each individual case, a little
over one point of hit rate on average, that either arm is defensible. The forecast-then-threshold
arm is used throughout this report's own warning-system results for a
reason beyond that narrow margin: it yields a concentration that can be
rethresholded for any future health policy without refitting, while a
classifier is welded to the threshold it was trained on.

The
supervisor's instruction to try several methods rather
than defaulting to ARIMA was the right one: it is what makes the negative
result at two and three days credible, and what surfaces the one day ahead
result that a project restricted to classical methods would never have found.

\section{Future Work}
\label{sec:future}

Three extensions follow: two from where this report's own weather work
stopped, and a third from the single-station limitation in
Section~\ref{sec:limitations}; a fourth, unrelated to either, follows from
the Fourier-harmonic check in that same section.
The threshold sweep has already been put through the weather-augmented
models (Section~\ref{sec:results-weather}), so the open thread is not
whether that comparison happened but what would change its answer: a real
forecast weather product, a numerical weather prediction for the days ahead
rather than the conditions already measured, is the stronger and more
useful claim for an operational system, and the one this project
deliberately did not make. A second is boundary layer height, unavailable
from \texttt{meteostat}, which would need a reanalysis product such as ERA5
and is the single variable most directly tied to the physical mechanism of
a particulate episode rather than a correlate of it; whether it would move
the threshold-sweep result more than wind speed and temperature did is an
open question precisely because the gain so far has been small.

A fourth, separate from either of those, follows directly from
Section~\ref{sec:limitations}'s Fourier-harmonic check: refitting the
recurrent network with four harmonics rather than two under the full
ten-seed rolling-origin evaluation, rather than the single validation
split used so far, would settle whether the gap to ARIMA at two and three
days ahead is substantially a consequence of that one previously
undocumented difference in Methodology's own specification, or whether
the bounded check's result does not survive a more demanding evaluation.

A fifth extension is independent of weather: repeating the analysis at a
second, independent station, ideally one inside the Central Pollution
Control Board network once its record lengthens, would test whether the
findings here are a property of Delhi air quality or an artefact of the one
diplomatic enclave monitor this project was restricted to. Until then, the
central recommendation stands on its own: a hazardous air quality warning
system should be designed around the alarm budget its operator can justify,
with the forecasting model treated as a secondary refinement rather than the
primary design choice.

\section{Chapter Summary}

Three research questions were asked and three were answered. Machine
learning earns a real but narrow place: the recurrent network alone beats
the classical benchmark, and only one day ahead. Forecasting the
concentration and then thresholding it has a modest, genuine edge over
classifying the exceedance directly, not a decisive one. And the decision
threshold, not the model, is what principally determines how many
hazardous days a warning system actually catches, a finding that held when
tested against a cleaning-threshold sensitivity check, against a
materially more accurate weather-augmented forecaster, and against a
doubled sample of the one model whose own training turned out not to be
fully reproducible. A project that set out to compare machine learning
against classical time series methods for a public health problem ends by
recommending that the comparison matters less than where the operator sets
the alarm.
